title: Grade 6 daily reading
overview: Read independently, with shared support for unfamiliar vocabulary and long sentences. Across 36 weeks, stories, complete poems, and natural-history prose move from close observation toward interpretation of irony, loyalty, memory, evidence, and the limits of a narrator’s knowledge. Reading budgets include rereading; discussion should return to exact words and allow defensible alternatives. Historical perspectives are examined in context. Timing and sequence are editorial suggestions, not measured reading levels.

progression.focus: Observe closely; test appearances against actions.
progression.rationale: Natural observations and accessible lyrics establish habits of citing details. Four complete fairy-tale narratives, spread across coherent episodes, and Cranford’s opening develop irony and memory across nights; the town’s comedy then turns to Captain Brown’s death and his daughter’s, told with restraint.

progression.focus: Follow a narrator through danger, uncertainty, and changing loyalties.
progression.rationale: Treasure Island’s opening eleven chapters develop sustained attention to clues, persuasion, and unreliable impressions. Contrasting poems and mountain observations invite slower rereading between narrative scenes.

progression.focus: Examine belonging, rules, and the responsibility to help.
progression.rationale: Mowgli’s stories test the difference between claimed membership and care in action, and “Tiger! Tiger!” resolves his vow against Shere Khan at the cost of a second rejection. Birds, landscapes, and poems extend attention to the difference between observing and assuming; discuss the historical narrator’s generalizations with support.

progression.focus: Connect private feeling with public behavior.
progression.rationale: Cranford’s restrained memories and losses require inference through omission, culminating in “Poor Peter,” the family story Miss Matty can tell only in the dark; the garden conflict in Rikki-tikki-tavi makes loyalty and consequences explicit. Dunbar and nature writers complicate easy readings of a cheerful surface.

progression.focus: Test an explanation against traces, testimony, and alternatives.
progression.rationale: Wind, storms, nests, islands, and Toomai’s remarkable report place explanation beside observable evidence. Reflective poems and the beginning of Cranford’s financial crisis increase demands on syntax and judgments about value.

progression.focus: Lead an interpretation, acknowledge uncertainty, and revise it with evidence.
progression.rationale: Cranford’s practical care completes its later arc, and Peter’s return answers the loss told in week 21. Wallace’s historical explanations, including his period classification of peoples, and Robinson’s compressed poems ask readers to distinguish evidence from analogy and assumption, recognize limits in a speaker’s knowledge, and defend alternatives. Shared support is useful for the sonnets.

days.title: Flight paths and first impressions — excerpt
days.challenge: Track contrasts among hovering, dropping, gliding and spiralling, then distinguish observed movement from imagined bird feelings.
days.focus: How close observation corrects an observer’s first impression of where birds land and how numerous they are.
days.context: Jefferies watches from a grassy earthwork on the English chalk downs. A fosse is a ditch and bennets are dried grass stems. The passage moves from one resting observer to several kinds of birds.

excerpt.locator: Chapter One; complete source paragraphs 11–18 in the accompanying source index; opens “The most commanding down is crowned with the grassy mound and”; closes “even in their restlessness, and do not jostle their neighbours.”.

questions.prompt: Why might someone looking for a lark or snipe search the wrong landing place?
facilitatorNotes: Both can move sideways close to the ground after appearing to drop; the visible descent does not reveal the final landing point. Connect the two examples rather than calling the observer careless.
evidence: This latter motion makes it difficult to tell where a lark actually does alight.

questions.prompt: What makes starlings seem more numerous, and what different evidence supports Jefferies’s estimate about larks?
facilitatorNotes: Starlings concentrate in spectacular flocks, while larks occur throughout a long walk. His estimate remains qualified by “probably”; neither observation is an exact census.
evidence: though scattered abroad they probably equal or exceed the starlings, who show so much more.

questions.prompt: At the end, where does Jefferies move from describing actions to interpreting feelings? What does that change add?
facilitatorNotes: Racing is visible, whereas envy and city-like anxiety are interpretations. These comparisons make the birds vivid and establish a contrast with placid larks, but readers may question whether human emotions explain the movements.
evidence: Each starling seems full of envy and emulation—eager to outstrip his fellow in the race for titbits;

days.title: Stars
days.challenge: Reread the contradictory image of stars marching while still, and follow the shift from solitude to honored witness.
days.focus: How scale, sensory detail, and personification turn aloneness into wonder.
days.context: Topaz names a golden-colored gemstone; aeons are immense spans of time. Read aloud after an initial silent reading.

excerpt.locator: Stars; complete poem, opening “Alone in the night” and closing “Of so much majesty.”.

questions.prompt: What does the pine detail add before the speaker looks upward?
facilitatorNotes: The spicy scent and stillness establish a bodily, quiet setting. Contrast this nearby sensation with the vast sky rather than treating the opening as empty scenery.
evidence: Spicy and still,

questions.prompt: How can the stars be both marching and still?
facilitatorNotes: The movement can describe the speaker’s imagined procession or slow celestial movement, while stillness captures the immediate view. Accept either supported interpretation; discuss the productive tension.
evidence:
I watch them marching
 Stately and still,

questions.prompt: Does being alone mean being unhappy in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: The final honor and majesty change how the solitary opening is understood: witnessing is a privilege. Acknowledge that quiet solitude can still feel emotionally mixed.
evidence:
Am honored to be
Witness

days.title: An ant’s interrupted highway — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a change in scale from inches to an explorer’s journey, then separate an experiment’s result from its explanation.
days.focus: How an interrupted ant trail becomes evidence in an argument about habit and correction.
days.context: The observer lies near the ditch of an old earthwork. He first follows one ant through grass, then recalls experiments on an established garden trail. Watling Street is used as a comparison for a busy road.
days.contentNote: The passage includes the period phrase “savage kings” in a comparison. That prejudiced label belongs to the historical author; it is not a description endorsed here.

excerpt.locator: Chapter One; complete source paragraphs 28–34 in the accompanying source index; opens “If we look closely into the grass here on the slope of the fosse it”; closes “and, observing where it fails, tries another place and succeeds.”.

questions.prompt: Choose two obstacles that are ordinary to a person but difficult for the ant. How does the description alter their scale?
facilitatorNotes: A horse’s hoofmark becomes a chasm, a grass fibre a bridge, and moss a difficult forest. The altered scale asks the reader to experience the journey from the insect’s position.
evidence: this lies like a bridge across a yawning chasm

questions.prompt: What exactly does Jefferies change in his trail experiment, and why does he stress that there is “no real obstruction”?
facilitatorNotes: He erases three inches of a worn trail without building a barrier. The ants pause despite an open route, which challenges the idea that an infallible instinct automatically guides them.
evidence: With a fragment of wood I rubbed out three inches of the path

questions.prompt: Does the ants’ eventual success prove Jefferies’s explanation about reason? Distinguish his observation and inference.
facilitatorNotes: He observes searching, mistakes and a renewed route; he infers error correction resembling reason. Those observations support a revisable account, but the passage does not rule out other means of following a trail.
evidence: Therefore it would seem that the ant works its way tentatively, and, observing where it fails, tries another place and succeeds.

days.title: The Selfish Giant — A garden without spring
days.challenge: Follow personified seasons without treating the tale as a literal weather explanation.
days.focus: The wall turns an ordinary property dispute into a visible emotional landscape.
days.context: In this fairy tale, a garden’s seasons respond to its owner’s choices.

excerpt.locator: The Selfish Giant — A garden without spring; source paragraphs 172–189 in downloaded transcription; opens “EVERY afternoon, as they were coming from school, the children used to go and play in the Giant”; closes “be the children’s playground for ever and ever.” He was really very sorry for what he had done.”.

questions.prompt: What changes between the children saying “How happy we are here!” and later saying “How happy we were there”?
facilitatorNotes: The past tense marks loss. Their shared garden becomes an inaccessible memory after the wall is built.
evidence: How happy we were there

questions.prompt: Why give the flower a response to the notice-board?
facilitatorNotes: Even the smallest living thing rejects the exclusion; nature becomes an active participant rather than a backdrop.
evidence: it slipped back into the ground again

questions.prompt: Why is melting an especially effective verb at this turning point?
facilitatorNotes: It links emotional change with the winter imagery. The cold heart and cold garden can begin to thaw together.
evidence: the Giant’s heart melted

days.title: The Selfish Giant — The return of the child
days.challenge: Notice how a repeated winter setting gains a different meaning after the Giant changes.
days.focus: Concrete acts of welcome prepare the tale’s symbolic ending.
days.context: The Giant has resolved to help the small boy and open the garden to everyone.
days.contentNote: The ending includes the Giant’s peaceful death and Christian allusions to crucifixion and Paradise.

excerpt.locator: The Selfish Giant — The return of the child; source paragraphs 190–204 in downloaded transcription; opens “So he crept downstairs and opened the front door quite softly, and went out into the garden. Bu”; closes “hat afternoon, they found the Giant lying dead under the tree, all covered with white blossoms.”.

questions.prompt: How does saying “It is your garden now” complete the change begun when the Giant sees the crying boy?
facilitatorNotes: He goes beyond feeling sorry: he removes the wall and gives the children a continuing place to play.
evidence: It is your garden now

questions.prompt: Why does winter no longer mean the same thing to the Giant?
facilitatorNotes: He now accepts waiting and renewal; the later winter does not represent his exclusion of others.
evidence: it was merely the Spring asleep

questions.prompt: How does the child’s answer redirect the Giant’s impulse to use a sword?
facilitatorNotes: It replaces retaliation with an image of sacrificial love; the wounds and Paradise identify the child within Christian symbolism.
evidence: these are the wounds of Love

days.title: Cranford, chapter I — The town’s unwritten rules
days.challenge: Distinguish affectionate amusement from simple approval of a community’s rules.
days.focus: A narrator can belong to a group while noticing the contradictions in its behavior.
days.context: Mary Smith describes a small English town whose social life is largely organized by women of limited means. Amazons refers to legendary women warriors.
days.contentNote: The narrator uses nineteenth-century assumptions about gender and social class. These are part of the society being portrayed.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter I — The town’s unwritten rules; source paragraphs 15–27 in downloaded transcription; opens “IN the first place, Cranford is in possession of the Amazons; all the holders of houses above a”; closes “s sister-in-law to the late Earl of Glenmire, although she did practise such “elegant economy.””.

questions.prompt: How does “without troubling themselves with unnecessary reasons or arguments” complicate the claim that the women know and manage everything?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator admires their competence while teasing their certainty; deciding questions is not the same as supporting a judgment.
evidence: without troubling themselves with unnecessary reasons or arguments

questions.prompt: What does the fifteen-minute visiting rule protect, and what does it prevent?
facilitatorNotes: It preserves social order and limits demands, but it also prevents absorbing conversation and spontaneous connection.
evidence: not allow yourself to forget it in conversation

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator repeat the layers of knowing about Mrs Forrester’s cakes?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone understands the pretense yet protects the hostess’s dignity. The elaborate wording makes their shared tact comic.
evidence: she knew, and we knew

days.title: Cranford, chapter I — Captain Brown breaks the rules
days.challenge: Follow the contrast between a reputation built by manners and one built by actions.
days.focus: A disruptive newcomer becomes useful to the community without deliberately seeking approval.
days.context: The town calls thrift “elegant economy” and avoids mentioning money. Captain Brown arrives with two daughters.
days.contentNote: Includes an injured cow and a suggestion of killing it; the owner instead clothes it to keep it warm.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter I — Captain Brown breaks the rules; source paragraphs 28–34 in downloaded transcription; opens ““Elegant economy!” How naturally one falls back into the phraseology of Cranford! There, econom”; closes “ly till she, with trembling nervous hands, had taken up her gown to walk through the wet roads.”.

questions.prompt: What does the candid label “sour-grapeism” add to the phrase “elegant economy”?
facilitatorNotes: It admits that taste may partly rationalize what people cannot afford; the narrator includes herself in the compromise.
evidence: sour-grapeism

questions.prompt: How does not noticing social signals help the Captain in this particular town?
facilitatorNotes: He continues being friendly and useful instead of answering slight with slight, so the initial hostility has little to feed on.
evidence: unaware of his popularity as he had been of the reverse

questions.prompt: Why end this portrait with the Captain helping his daughter after church?
facilitatorNotes: The small, patient act supplies evidence of care beneath his loud manner; it qualifies judgments based on noise or appearance.
evidence: waited patiently

days.title: Cranford, chapter I — A quarrel over books
days.challenge: Separate reasons about writing from defenses of rank, identity, and family habit.
days.focus: A literary disagreement becomes personal because a preferred author supports a character’s self-image.
days.context: Captain Brown joins a Cranford party and praises Dickens’s Pickwick Papers. Miss Jenkyns favors Samuel Johnson.
days.contentNote: The source contains a censored oath. Class prejudice against shopkeepers is portrayed through the town’s reactions.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter I — A quarrel over books; source paragraphs 35–57 in downloaded transcription; opens “I wonder what the Cranford ladies did with Captain Brown at their parties. We had often rejoice”; closes “ was inexorable. The next day she made the remark I have mentioned about Miss Jessie’s dimples.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Captain’s behavior at tea show that the later quarrel might make us overlook?
facilitatorNotes: He notices practical needs and quietly helps; intellectual disagreement does not cancel his demonstrated consideration.
evidence: lessened the pretty maid-servant’s labour

questions.prompt: Why is the Captain’s quiet question a pointed answer to the objection to publishing in numbers?
facilitatorNotes: Johnson’s Rambler also appeared serially. The question exposes a standard applied differently to a favored author.
evidence: How was the _Rambler_ published

questions.prompt: Why does criticism of Johnson’s style feel like criticism of Miss Jenkyns herself?
facilitatorNotes: She has modeled her own letters on him and treats that skill as a distinction; taste is bound to personal pride.
evidence: I have formed my own style upon it

days.title: Cranford, chapter II — The Captain and his daughters
days.challenge: Track how the narrator conveys shock and grief through other people’s actions, reported speech and small objects rather than direct description.
days.focus: Cranford’s comedy of manners turns to loss, and the same habits—Miss Jenkyns’s Johnson, the new carpet, the bonnet—now carry grief.
days.context: Months after the quarrel over Dickens’s Pickwick and Dr Johnson, Captain Brown’s elder daughter, Miss Brown, is dying after a long illness, and her younger sister, Jessie, nurses her. Miss Jenkyns has quietly been sending them small kindnesses. Mr Hoggins is the town doctor. Later in the chapter, beyond this excerpt, Jessie finds a home and marries an old suitor, Major Gordon.
days.contentNote: Captain Brown is killed by a train while saving a small child; the carter’s report is brief. Miss Brown then dies of her illness, with prayers and last words at her bedside.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter II — The Captain and his daughters; source paragraphs 72–99 in downloaded transcription; opens “Captain Brown called one day to thank Miss Jenkyns for many little kindnesses,”; closes “few moments more Miss Brown lay calm and still—never to sorrow or murmur more.”.

questions.prompt: Miss Jenkyns’s household is usually strict about order. What does the detail that the carter stood “with his wet boots on the new carpet, and no one regarded it” show about the room at that moment?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone is too shocked to notice the rules that normally govern the drawing-room; Gaskell measures grief by what people stop seeing. Some students may also notice that a working man has been brought straight into the best room, so class boundaries are briefly forgotten too.
evidence: with his wet boots on the new carpet, and no one regarded it

questions.prompt: Miss Jenkyns cries, “God pardon me, if ever I have spoken contemptuously to the Captain!” Yet when the newspaper reports that he was reading ‘Pickwick,’ she sighs, “Poor, dear, infatuated man!” Are these two responses consistent?
facilitatorNotes: Both can be true at once: she feels real remorse for her coldness, yet her literary opinions have not moved at all. Some readers find the second remark comic or petty; others find it touching, because her grief speaks in her usual voice. Ask students which reading the evidence supports better.
evidence: God pardon me, if ever I have spoken contemptuously to the Captain!
Poor, dear, infatuated man!

questions.prompt: Why does Jessie insist that her sister be told only that their father has gone on “a short journey on railway business,” and how does her last speech to Miss Brown change the meaning of that decision?
facilitatorNotes: Jessie protects a dying sister from a shock she believes would make her last days miserable. At the end she tells the truth as comfort: the father is waiting, and “knows now.” The concealment becomes a gift, though students may still debate whether withholding the truth was right.
evidence: a short journey on railway business
he has gone before you to the place where the weary are at rest

questions.prompt: In the middle of the funeral preparations, the narrator admits that Miss Jenkyns’s bonnet reminded her of a helmet. Why might Gaskell include a comic thought in the saddest part of the chapter?
facilitatorNotes: It is honest about how minds wander in grief, and it keeps Cranford’s voice consistent. The helmet image also fits Miss Jenkyns’s armour-like firmness, which turns out to support Jessie “with a tender, indulgent firmness.” Some readers may find the joke jarring; that reaction is worth discussing too.
evidence: I no sooner saw the bonnet than I was reminded of a helmet
with a tender, indulgent firmness

days.title: Only in Sleep
days.challenge: Separate the remembered children, the adult speaker, and the unanswered possibility of appearing in someone else’s dream.
days.focus: Dreams suspend time but cannot establish what others remember.
days.context: The speaker meets childhood companions in sleep. Use the two named children and the doll-house to map the remembered scene before interpreting the final question.

excerpt.locator: Only in Sleep; complete poem, opening “Only in sleep I see their faces,” and closing “And for them am I too a child?”.

questions.prompt: How do Louise and Annie remain distinct rather than becoming anonymous childhood friends?
facilitatorNotes: Their different hairstyles individualize memory: braided brown hair versus warm, wild ringlets. The small details make the dream feel particular.
evidence: Louise comes back with her brown hair braided,

questions.prompt: What does the unchanged doll-house do for the poem’s treatment of time?
facilitatorNotes: It anchors the dream in an old physical arrangement that has not aged; the dream restores a setting as well as faces.
evidence: And the doll-house stood at the turn of the stair.

questions.prompt: What uncertainty remains in the final two lines?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker cannot know whether the friends dream of the speaker or preserve the same child-image. Accept interpretations of mutual connection or loneliness that respect the question’s uncertainty.
evidence: Do they, too, dream of me, I wonder,

days.title: The Happy Prince — A statue learns to see
days.challenge: Separate what the townspeople assume from what the Prince reveals about his life.
days.focus: Wilde uses a change of viewpoint to unsettle the meaning of happiness.
days.context: A fairy tale opens with a statue admired by the whole town. A migrating swallow stops beside it.
days.contentNote: The story includes poverty, illness, and a statue speaking after the Prince’s death.

excerpt.locator: The Happy Prince — A statue learns to see; source paragraphs 19–50 in downloaded transcription; opens “HIGH above the city, on a tall column, stood the statue of the Happy Prince. He was gilded all ”; closes ““Thank you, little Swallow,” said the Prince.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Councillor’s correction reveal about his reason for praising the statue?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to appear both artistic and practical; the praise advertises himself as much as it describes the statue.
evidence: only not quite so useful

questions.prompt: Why does the Prince qualify his own claim to have been happy?
facilitatorNotes: His palace pleasures depended on not seeing suffering. The qualification invites readers to distinguish comfort from awareness.
evidence: if pleasure be happiness

questions.prompt: What changes the Swallow’s decision, and what has not yet changed about him?
facilitatorNotes: Pity moves him to help, though he still intends to travel and continues judging events by his own comfort.
evidence: but I will stay with you for one night

days.title: The Happy Prince — Two deliveries
days.challenge: Track the difference between the reader’s knowledge and the recipients’ explanations.
days.focus: Contrasts between comfortable observers and hidden labor create irony.
days.context: The Swallow has agreed to carry the Prince’s ruby to a seamstress whose child is ill.
days.contentNote: The passing description of Jews handling money repeats a historical stereotype; it is not an account of a whole community. Discuss how an incidental image can carry prejudice.

excerpt.locator: The Happy Prince — Two deliveries; source paragraphs 51–68 in downloaded transcription; opens “So the Swallow picked out the great ruby from the Prince’s sword, and flew away with it in his ”; closes “ cried; “this is from some great admirer. Now I can finish my play,” and he looked quite happy.”.

questions.prompt: How does the court lady’s complaint change when we place it beside the sleeping mother?
facilitatorNotes: The mother sleeps from exhaustion while sewing the dress; the complaint exposes the comfortable woman’s ignorance.
evidence: the seamstresses are so lazy

questions.prompt: What is amusing, and troubling, about the public’s response to the Professor’s letter?
facilitatorNotes: People treat obscurity as authority. His learned notice misses the acts of care that explain the bird’s presence.
evidence: it was full of so many words that they could not understand

questions.prompt: Why does the playwright’s explanation of the sapphire matter?
facilitatorNotes: He benefits without knowing the sacrifice or the giver. Gratitude and accurate understanding are shown to be different.
evidence: this is from some great admirer

days.title: The Happy Prince — Seeing for another
days.challenge: Connect repeated promises to an increasingly costly decision.
days.focus: The bird becomes an observer of suffering rather than merely a visitor.
days.context: The Prince has given away a ruby and one sapphire eye. The Swallow again plans to leave before winter.
days.contentNote: Includes a threat of parental violence and hungry children. The Swallow’s travel fantasy uses exoticized images of African peoples; treat it as the tale’s imagined geography, not reliable cultural description.

excerpt.locator: The Happy Prince — Seeing for another; source paragraphs 69–85 in downloaded transcription; opens “The next day the Swallow flew down to the harbour. He sat on the mast of a large vessel and wat”; closes “ grew rosier, and they laughed and played games in the street. “We have bread now!” they cried.”.

questions.prompt: How does giving away the second eye alter the partnership?
facilitatorNotes: The Prince now depends on the Swallow’s sight; the Swallow’s voluntary loyalty replaces a temporary errand.
evidence: You are blind now

questions.prompt: Why does the Prince interrupt the marvelous travel stories by saying that there is no mystery so great as misery?
facilitatorNotes: He redirects wonder toward nearby people. Readers may discuss whether wonder and responsibility can coexist.
evidence: There is no Mystery so great as Misery

questions.prompt: What does repeating “Leaf after leaf” make us notice about the exchange?
facilitatorNotes: The statue’s beauty diminishes gradually while children gain food; the parallel clauses trace the same gold in two places.
evidence: Leaf after leaf

days.title: The Happy Prince — What the city throws away
days.challenge: Read the ending through two competing standards of value.
days.focus: The city’s judgments reverse the story’s understanding of beauty and usefulness.
days.context: The statue has given away its jewels and gold, and the Swallow has stayed with it into winter.
days.contentNote: The Swallow dies and the statue is melted. The ending uses Christian images of God, angels, and Paradise.

excerpt.locator: The Happy Prince — What the city throws away; source paragraphs 86–103 in downloaded transcription; opens “Then the snow came, and after the snow came the frost. The streets looked as if they were made ”; closes “ little bird shall sing for evermore, and in my city of gold the Happy Prince shall praise me.””.

questions.prompt: How does the winter description combine beauty with danger?
facilitatorNotes: Bright silver and crystal are attractive, but daggers suggest harm; the bird experiences the lethal side of the lovely scene.
evidence: crystal daggers

questions.prompt: What evidence from this ending challenges the Art Professor’s judgment?
facilitatorNotes: The discarded heart and bird are judged precious in the final scene; usefulness cannot be measured by decoration alone.
evidence: As he is no longer beautiful he is no longer useful

questions.prompt: Why end the officials’ discussion with their identical demands?
facilitatorNotes: Their agreement collapses into rivalry when a reward is available. The repeated words contrast with the Prince’s gifts.
evidence: Of myself

days.title: Redbirds
days.challenge: Follow the poem’s movement from remembered birds through a broad landscape back to a question the speaker cannot answer.
days.focus: Refrain and place details preserve affection while admitting distance.
days.context: The place names belong to the speaker’s remembered landscape. Read the opening and ending together, then trace the intervening river scene.

excerpt.locator: Redbirds; complete poem, opening “Redbirds, redbirds,” and closing “On Saxton's Hill?”.

questions.prompt: What does calling the birds’ sound a honey-call suggest beyond loudness?
facilitatorNotes: Honey suggests sweetness or pleasure; the metaphor gives a sound the sensory quality of taste.
evidence: What a honey-call you had

questions.prompt: How does the river enlarge the scene beyond the birds?
facilitatorNotes: Its southward sweep and movement around bluffs connect small calls to a grand, continuous landscape. The stately motion contrasts with the brief recalled day.
evidence:
And proud river sweeping
 Southward to the sea,

questions.prompt: How does the final question change the repeated address to the birds?
facilitatorNotes: The opening recalls confidently, while the ending admits the present is unknown. The refrain becomes a way of reaching toward a place now distant.
evidence: Are you singing still

days.title: Water on a dry ridge — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect several kinds of evidence while noticing words that distinguish a proposed explanation from a demonstrated result.
days.focus: The argument linking a hilltop pond, mist, frozen branches and a possible ancient landscape.
days.context: Jefferies has been considering how people at an ancient hilltop earthwork might have obtained water. This excerpt introduces a modern livestock pond and asks what it might suggest about earlier conditions.
days.contentNote: The explanation is Jefferies’s own historical reasoning, not a modern hydrological finding. He describes tasting the pond water.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Two; complete source paragraphs 60–64 in the accompanying source index; opens “Scarcely a quarter of a mile from the earthwork, and on a level with”; closes “and near the foot of the down at the rear of the entrenchment.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the pond’s remaining water surprising to the observer?
facilitatorNotes: It lies exposed at the top of a ridge, without an apparent spring or substantial watershed. A reader should connect those features to the expectation that summer heat would empty it.
evidence: neither is there a spring or any other apparent source of supply.

questions.prompt: How do the ice-coated beech branches contribute to his explanation?
facilitatorNotes: They make otherwise invisible atmospheric moisture visible and substantial. He uses their ice as support for the possibility of condensation, although this does not by itself measure how much water reaches the pond.
evidence: it becomes more easy to understand the amount of water which an intangible vapour may carry with it

questions.prompt: Which wording limits his conclusion about the ancient fort? Why does that qualification matter?
facilitatorNotes: “If” the hills were forested and “it appears possible” identify a hypothesis. The modern pond and winter ice are observations; the old landscape and water supply are a reconstruction needing further evidence.
evidence: if these hills were once clothed with forest, as previously suggested, it appears possible

days.title: The hill that seemed to grow — excerpt
days.challenge: Reconstruct the observer’s changing viewpoint and distinguish an illusion from the evidence that corrects it.
days.focus: How a limited frame can mislead the eye even after the mind recognizes an explanation.
days.context: After a rainy day, Jefferies walks beside a hedge below familiar hills. The episode begins during a hunting outing but centres on an unexpected visual illusion.
days.contentNote: The opening mentions carrying a gun to shoot rabbits; no shooting or injury occurs in this selected episode.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Two; complete source paragraphs 70–74 in the accompanying source index; opens “A long day of rain is often followed by a moderately fine evening—the”; closes “the cloud was lighter in colour than the hill to which it clung.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the apparently taller hill trouble Jefferies rather than simply convince him?
facilitatorNotes: The outline, barn and trees are familiar, but the apparent height conflicts with repeated experience. The conflict makes him return for another look.
evidence: somehow it seemed singular that the great elevation of this down should never previously have been so apparent.

questions.prompt: What changes when he climbs onto the hedge bank?
facilitatorNotes: He can see the neighbouring ridges at once instead of a narrow isolated section. Their normal height reveals the cloud’s role in enlarging the central hill.
evidence: from the elevation of the mound the whole range of hills could be seen at the same time.

questions.prompt: Why is the second similar illusion less convincing, and what does that tell us about the first?
facilitatorNotes: An open viewpoint and a lighter cloud make the border easier to distinguish. The first deception depended jointly on a restricted frame and matching colours; recognizing it intellectually did not instantly change what his eye saw.
evidence: because seen from a more open spot, allowing an extended view of the range, and because the cloud was lighter in colour

days.title: Following a spring through time — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow movement down a stream while recognizing shifts from physical description to speculation about deep time.
days.focus: How small visible details lead to larger explanations about landscape, living things and hidden drainage.
days.context: A coombe is a narrow valley in the chalk hills. Jefferies begins at three tiny springs below an ancient earthwork and follows their joined stream toward the valley.
days.contentNote: Plant identifications, medicinal customs and claims about living creatures reflect an 1879 text. They are subjects for reading and evidence discussion, not foraging or health instructions.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Three; complete source paragraphs 109–117 in the accompanying source index; opens “In the narrow valley, far below the frowning ramparts of the ancient”; closes “current winds its way—so deep that no cattle can get down to drink.”.

questions.prompt: How does sound change as the three threads of water become a stream?
facilitatorNotes: The source oozes silently; farther down a murmur becomes audible as the current crosses stones and steeper ground. The changing sound helps the reader follow increasing movement and volume.
evidence: gently oozing forth without a sound.

questions.prompt: Why does the empty snail shell turn his attention toward immense stretches of time?
facilitatorNotes: One shell stands for a once-living creature and innumerable ancestors; its smallness contrasts with the accumulated history of life. Readers may emphasize wonder, mortality or continuity if they connect their interpretation to this movement.
evidence: If time is measured by the duration of life, reckoned by their short spans eternity upon eternity has gone by.

questions.prompt: What solves the puzzle of a brook growing without visible tributaries, and which further claim remains hypothetical?

days.focus: A small household challenges a stronger intruder’s claim.
days.context: In this animal fantasy, a wolf family encounters a human child while a tiger hunts nearby. The jungle has an imagined code of laws.
days.contentNote: Includes threatened predation on a child, fire, and disability-based insults. Colonial racial categories and a stigmatizing description of rabies belong to the historical fantasy, not reliable social or scientific accounts.

excerpt.locator: Mowgli’s Brothers — A child at the cave; source paragraphs 66–112 in downloaded transcription; opens “IT was seven o'clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from ”; closes “"But what will our Pack say?" said Father Wolf.”.

questions.prompt: Why are Tabaqui’s compliments not simple kindness?
facilitatorNotes: He knows the wolves regard praise of their cubs as unlucky and deliberately unsettles them. Polite words conceal mischief.
evidence: it pleased him to see Mother and Father Wolf look uncomfortable

questions.prompt: How does the narrator distinguish the animals’ stated reason for sparing humans from their practical reason?
facilitatorNotes: The stated reason invokes fairness to weak creatures; the practical reason is fear of human retaliation. The contrast questions self-flattering explanations.
evidence: The reason the beasts give among themselves

questions.prompt: Why does Father Wolf’s final question keep the rescue from being a complete resolution?
facilitatorNotes: The family can protect and choose the child, but membership also requires the wider pack’s acceptance. Private care meets public rules.
evidence: But what will our Pack say?

days.title: Mowgli’s Brothers — The council’s decision
days.challenge: Compare different reasons for making the same decision.
days.focus: Rules, generosity, self-interest, and foresight all shape acceptance.
days.context: Mother and Father Wolf have protected Mowgli from Shere Khan. Now they must present him with their cubs to the pack council.
days.contentNote: The fantasy’s laws include death penalties and violent removal of aging leaders; these are features of its imagined society.

excerpt.locator: Mowgli’s Brothers — The council’s decision; source paragraphs 113–139 in downloaded transcription; opens “The Law of the Jungle lays down very clearly that any wolf may, when he marries, withdraw from ”; closes “Mowgli was entered into the Seeonee wolf-pack for the price of a bull and on Baloo's good word.”.

questions.prompt: What does the rule requiring supporters beyond the parents accomplish in this scene?
facilitatorNotes: It makes acceptance a community responsibility rather than only a family wish. It creates the need for Baloo’s and Bagheera’s intervention.
evidence: he must be spoken for by at least two members

questions.prompt: How does the wolves’ question complicate their agreement to accept Mowgli?
facilitatorNotes: Their attention to food suggests appetite helps win consent. Acceptance does not necessarily mean they share the rescuers’ care for him.
evidence: Where is the bull, Bagheera?

questions.prompt: What future concern enters the scene just after the child is accepted?
facilitatorNotes: Akela’s strength and leadership will end. Bagheera suggests Mowgli may someday help, linking a present act of protection to future vulnerability.
evidence: none can hope to lead the Pack forever

days.title: Mowgli’s Brothers — The mark of the collar
days.challenge: Read a familiar life from two characters’ different perspectives.
days.focus: Belonging feels secure to one character and endangered to another.
days.context: Years pass. Mowgli learns from the wolves, Baloo, and Bagheera, while Shere Khan gains influence among younger members of the pack.
days.contentNote: Includes animal killing, captivity, threats, and Mowgli’s mistreatment of Tabaqui. Species hierarchies and human superiority are part of the fantasy’s assumptions.

excerpt.locator: Mowgli’s Brothers — The mark of the collar; source paragraphs 140–163 in downloaded transcription; opens “Now you must be content to skip ten or eleven whole years, and only guess at all the wonderful ”; closes “d not know these things," said Mowgli, sullenly; and he frowned under his heavy black eyebrows.”.

questions.prompt: What does comparing jungle sounds with office work tell us about Mowgli’s education?
facilitatorNotes: He reads surroundings as meaningful practical information. The comparison makes apparently wild experience a form of skilled learning.
evidence: the work of his office means to a business man

questions.prompt: What evidence supports Mowgli’s claim of brotherhood, and why may it fail to protect him?
facilitatorNotes: He has lived by their law and cared for their injuries. Bagheera explains that resentment and manipulated group boundaries can outweigh those facts.
evidence: Surely they are my brothers!

questions.prompt: How does Bagheera’s hidden mark change our understanding of his help to Mowgli?
facilitatorNotes: His own captivity gives him a personal connection to a creature living outside its original world. The disclosure turns a powerful protector into someone with a vulnerable history.
evidence: the mark of the collar

days.title: Effusion
days.challenge: Trace the transition from exhausted labor and doubtful writing to a concrete promise of care, separating recognition from wealth.
days.focus: The speaker measures success through reciprocity with parents rather than applause alone.
days.context: An effusion is an outpouring of feeling. The speaker recalls hardship before describing hoped-for and present help for parents.
days.contentNote: Describes poverty, hunger, and parental hardship without graphic detail.

excerpt.locator: Effusion; complete poem, opening “Ah, little did I think in time that’s past,” and closing “Nor think I’m happy till ye both are blest.”.

questions.prompt: How does writing at night complicate the idea that poetry is effortless inspiration?
facilitatorNotes: The aching body and weary hand show writing added to demanding physical work. The poem places art inside labor.
evidence: And sitting down with weary hand to write;

questions.prompt: Why describe the parents breaking the same crust again?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated division dramatizes how little there is and how much they surrender; the action supplies evidence for the speaker’s gratitude.
evidence: And though want pinch’d, the remnant broke again,

questions.prompt: How does the final sixpence echo the earlier bread?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker promises to divide scarce money and ultimately give it all, repeating the parents’ generosity in a new direction. It is a personal pledge, not a universal financial rule.
evidence: My last-earn’d sixpence will I break with thee:

days.title: A farmhouse’s household memory — excerpt
days.challenge: Infer the importance of objects and dates that the family treats as ordinary or universally familiar.
days.focus: How a house becomes an archive of continuity and change.
days.context: Wick Farm stands alone beyond the village. The observer enters a household whose family has occupied the same homestead for several generations.
days.contentNote: The stored objects include weapons, and family memories mention violence during machine-breaking disturbances and wars. The passage describes no battle scene.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Seven; complete source paragraphs 237–243 in the accompanying source index; opens “The stream, after leaving the village and the washpool, rushes”; closes “costume; the smock-frock lingered longest, but even that is going.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the family’s way of dating events unusual to an outsider?
facilitatorNotes: Private events such as buying the Foremeads become shared historical landmarks inside the family, even after ninety years. Their familiarity makes distant time seem close.
evidence: as if that transaction, which took place ninety years before, was of such importance that it must necessarily be still known to all the world.

questions.prompt: Why might the family use old china at tea yet refuse to sell it?
facilitatorNotes: Practical familiarity does not mean lack of attachment. Its place in the household matters more to them than the connoisseur’s artistic or monetary judgment.
evidence: These have been there of old time: they shall remain still.

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph complicate the impression that this household never changes?
facilitatorNotes: Breeds of cattle, sheep and other animals have changed, housing practices differ, and clothing is disappearing. Memory preserves continuity while revealing substantial change.
evidence: the very races of animals have changed or been supplanted.

days.title: Mowgli’s Brothers — The Red Flower
days.challenge: Trace how naming and familiarity change an object’s apparent danger.
days.focus: Mowgli crosses a boundary by learning from people he scarcely knows.
days.context: Bagheera fears the pack will turn against Mowgli when its aging leader fails. He suggests obtaining something from the human village.
days.contentNote: Mowgli takes a pot of fire from a village child and learns to tend it. Includes a failed hunt.

excerpt.locator: Mowgli’s Brothers — The Red Flower; source paragraphs 164–185 in downloaded transcription; opens “"What is the Law of the Jungle? Strike first and then give tongue. By thy very carelessness the”; closes “ouncil Rock, he laughed till Tabaqui ran away. Then Mowgli went to the Council, still laughing.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the animals call fire the Red Flower instead of naming it directly?
facilitatorNotes: The beautiful substitute reflects fear and distance. Their language makes fire both mysterious and recognizable by its color and shape.
evidence: invents a hundred ways of describing it

questions.prompt: How does observing the village child alter Mowgli’s confidence?
facilitatorNotes: An ordinary human action makes the task seem possible. His reasoning comes from comparison, though it does not remove fire’s actual dangers.
evidence: If a cub can do it, there is nothing to fear

questions.prompt: Why does Mowgli hesitate over the memory of being near fire?
facilitatorNotes: A dim experience before his wolf upbringing returns without certainty. His identity contains traces of a life he cannot fully recover.
evidence: if it is not a dream

days.title: Mowgli’s Brothers — Law under pressure
days.challenge: Test repeated accusations against the actions offered in evidence.
days.focus: A community’s promises are tested when keeping them becomes unpopular.
days.context: Akela has failed in a hunt. At the council, Shere Khan presses the wolves to surrender Mowgli, while Bagheera and Akela defend him.
days.contentNote: Includes explicit threats of death and references to attacks on children. “Dead Wolf” is the pack’s cruel name for a leader who has failed a hunt.

excerpt.locator: Mowgli’s Brothers — Law under pressure; source paragraphs 186–205 in downloaded transcription; opens “Akela the Lone Wolf lay by the side of his rock as a sign that the leadership of the Pack was o”; closes “Now the business is in thy hands," said Bagheera to Mowgli. "_We_ can do no more except fight."”.

questions.prompt: How does Akela answer the claim that Mowgli has no place among the wolves?
facilitatorNotes: He cites shared life, useful work, and obedience. He bases membership on conduct rather than species alone.
evidence: he has broken no word of the Law of the Jungle

questions.prompt: How do the wolves and Bagheera understand the old bull payment differently?
facilitatorNotes: The wolves see a consumed benefit; Bagheera sees a continuing pledge. Their dispute concerns whether an agreement survives the immediate reward.
evidence: What do we care for bones ten years old?

questions.prompt: What makes Akela’s offer a sacrifice, and why does it still fail to persuade the pack?
facilitatorNotes: He gives up his right of defense to protect Mowgli, potentially saving several opponents. The repeated cry that Mowgli is human refuses to engage his argument.
evidence: I will die without fighting

days.title: Mowgli’s Brothers — Victory and farewell
days.challenge: Consider what a character gains and loses in the same scene.
days.focus: Power can secure safety without restoring belonging.
days.context: The council has rejected Mowgli’s defenders. He still holds the pot of fire that the animals fear.
days.contentNote: Mowgli burns and threatens animals while forcing his escape. The ending includes grief and separation; his wolf family continues to love him.

excerpt.locator: Mowgli’s Brothers — Victory and farewell; source paragraphs 206–225 in downloaded transcription; opens “Mowgli stood upright--the fire-pot in his hands. Then he stretched out his arms, and yawned in ”; closes “ went down the hillside alone to the crops to meet those mysterious things that are called men.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mowgli qualify his plan to go to humans?
facilitatorNotes: The pack has rejected him, but he does not yet know human society. Biology alone has not supplied a felt home.
evidence: if they be my own people

questions.prompt: What boundary does Mowgli set even while angrily using his new power?
facilitatorNotes: He promises not to bring human retaliation on the pack and protects Akela. His rage contains a continuing sense of obligation, though his violence remains troubling.
evidence: I will not betray ye to men as ye have betrayed me

questions.prompt: Why describe humans as mysterious things in the final sentence?
facilitatorNotes: The narration stays close to Mowgli’s jungle viewpoint. Familiar people become strangers, emphasizing uncertainty after the affectionate family farewell.
evidence: those mysterious things that are called men

days.title: Entering a hidden meadow — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow changes of scale from a whole meadow to moss cups, then connect delight with an argument about scientific attention.
days.focus: Whether pleasure in a place can sharpen rather than weaken observation.
days.context: Muir invites the reader to imagine walking from Tuolumne Soda Springs into a meadow concealed by forest. A moraine can form a dam behind which a lake once stood.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, The Glacier Meadows; complete source paragraphs 231–236 in the accompanying source index; opens “One of the very finest of the thousands I have enjoyed lies”; closes “as they are presented throughout the more marked seasons of the year.”.

questions.prompt: How does the approach through the forest prepare the meadow’s sudden appearance?
facilitatorNotes: Fallen trunks, tall grasses and obscured peaks limit movement and sight; vertical sunshine signals the opening before the purple lawn is revealed.
evidence: vertical bars of sunshine are seen ahead between the brown shafts of the pines

questions.prompt: What changes when the observer parts the grasses rather than merely walking through them?
facilitatorNotes: The meadow becomes branching stems, floral structures, moss cups and an insect-sized landscape. The shift reveals complexity hidden in the general smooth lawn.
evidence: Beneath the lowest leaves you discover a fairy realm of mosses

questions.prompt: What evidence does Muir offer against the claim that enjoyment impairs scientific work?
facilitatorNotes: He turns from pleasure to tracing the glacier, dam, ice-pushed stones and former lake hollows. These are concrete observations that he says enjoyment helps him perceive.
evidence: the mind is fertilized and stimulated and developed like sun-fed plants.

days.title: The starling’s imagined speech — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish real sounds and movements from the author’s invented interpretation of a bird’s dialogue.
days.focus: The uses and limits of giving a wild bird a human voice.
days.context: The old farmhouse’s deep thatch provides nesting holes. From its chimneys and a nearby ash tree, starlings call to one another and travel toward feeding grounds.
days.contentNote: The starling’s quoted speech is Jefferies’s imaginative personification, not a recorded translation of animal language. It includes a passing reference to shooting.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Eight; complete source paragraphs 280–286 in the accompanying source index; opens “Wick farmhouse is thatched, and has many gables hidden with ivy. In”; closes “of mortar under the eaves, to which the owners have not returned.”.

questions.prompt: What observed features of the starling’s voice make Jefferies imagine conversation rather than a repeated song?
facilitatorNotes: He notes a wide pitch range, variations, clucking and direct orientation toward other birds. These observations motivate the imagined speech without proving its exact words.
evidence: he runs a complete gamut, with ‘shakes,’ trills, tremulous vibrations, every possible variation.

questions.prompt: In the invented speech, why would recently grazed or mown ground interest the birds?
facilitatorNotes: Shorter vegetation exposes food previously hard to reach. The fanciful invitation contains an explanation linking farm work, cattle and the birds’ feeding opportunities.
evidence: it was too long for us before, but where they have eaten we can get at the ground comfortably.

questions.prompt: What changes when the passage moves from the speech to a flash across the reader’s book?
facilitatorNotes: The voice gives way to an optical observation: wings interrupt sunlight and create a flash. Readers may see a move from imaginative explanation to sensory evidence, while both make ordinary birds surprising.
evidence: the swift succession of light and shadow as the wings intercept the rays of the sun

days.title: The Poet’s Mind
days.challenge: Track the shift from a flowing mind to a guarded garden, asking what the elaborate boundary protects and excludes.
days.focus: An extended metaphor defends creative receptivity against a hostile observer.
days.context: A sophist here is the speaker’s name for a shallow disputant.
days.contentNote: Contains figurative death and blighting imagery, religious language, and hostile address to an imagined critic.

excerpt.locator: The Poet’s Mind; complete poem, opening “Vex not thou the poet’s mind” and closing “It would shrink to the earth if you came in.”.

questions.prompt: Why begin with clear water rather than a locked or mysterious chamber?
facilitatorNotes: The mind is represented as bright and flowing even while the outsider cannot fathom it; difficulty of understanding need not mean inner obscurity.
evidence: Flowing like a crystal river;

questions.prompt: What do frost and the frozen sneer imply about the visitor’s effect?
facilitatorNotes: Hostility is imagined as killing the garden’s living growth. The contrast with warm, scented flowers makes criticism a climate rather than only an argument.
evidence: There is frost in your breath

questions.prompt: Does calling the visitor’s ears dull explain the barrier or merely assert it?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker insists the song is full and clear yet inaccessible to this listener. Discuss whether that persuasively describes unreceptiveness or risks dismissing all disagreement.
evidence: You never would hear it; your ears are so dull;

days.title: Birds at an open window — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare several birds’ responses to the same human space, noticing qualified explanations.
days.focus: What repeated visits reveal, and what an observer can only infer, about attention and food.
days.context: A pear tree grows against the farmhouse wall beside an open bedroom window. The branches allow small birds to approach the room.
days.contentNote: One bird is briefly immobilized by fright and later flies away; the author also mentions fighting and threats to birds. His explanations of animal perception are historical inferences.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Eight; complete source paragraphs 299–305 in the accompanying source index; opens “The window of a room in which I used to sleep overlooked the orchard,”; closes “in the latter doubtless afford them insects from under the dead bark.”.

questions.prompt: Which features could make the window and old books attractive to the wren?
facilitatorNotes: Decayed wood contains insect holes and sawdust, while worm-eaten books may hold food. Jefferies marks the explanation as possible rather than reporting that he saw every feeding event.
evidence: Perhaps these formed an attraction to the wren.

questions.prompt: How do the robin’s increasing confidence and the frightened tomtit challenge a simple label such as “tame birds”?
facilitatorNotes: The robin becomes bolder after repeated undisturbed visits; the tomtit becomes helpless after a sudden entrance. Behaviour depends on circumstances, and apparently safe movement can change abruptly.
evidence: Encouraged by finding that no one disturbed him, at last he grew bold enough

questions.prompt: Explain the author’s use of the saying that the eye sees what it comes to see. Which detail supports it?
facilitatorNotes: A bird may notice a tiny food item while failing to notice a large nearby person. The saying connects selective attention in birds and people; it is an interpretation of contrasting observations.
evidence: Their eyes, ever on the watch for food, instantly detect a tiny creeping thing several yards distant

days.title: The Blackbird
days.challenge: Separate observed feeding and changing song from the speaker’s moral accusation against the bird.
days.focus: A garden encounter becomes a debatable lesson about abundance and obligation.
days.context: Espaliers and standards are trained and upright fruit trees; black-hearts are cherries and a jenneting is an early apple.
days.contentNote: Mentions people shooting birds and threatens future want; no animal injury is described.

excerpt.locator: The Blackbird; complete poem, opening “O blackbird! sing me something well:” and closing “Caught in the frozen palms of Spring.”.

questions.prompt: What does repeating that the garden is all thine establish before the complaint?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker stresses generosity and plenty, making the later demand for song sound like an expected return.
evidence: All thine, against the garden wall.

questions.prompt: How do golden bill and silver tongue measure the bird in different ways?
facilitatorNotes: The bill damages fruit while the tongue signifies valued song. Metallic beauty can describe both an admired gift and a destructive tool.
evidence: A golden bill! the silver tongue,

questions.prompt: Is plenty corrupts the melody an observation or a judgment?
facilitatorNotes: The bird’s changed song is observed, but corruption assigns a moral cause. Readers may see satire of people projected onto a bird rather than reliable animal explanation.
evidence: Plenty corrupts the melody

days.title: The blackbird as sentinel and singer — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow changes between alarm calls and song, and assess how human character comparisons shape a description.
days.focus: A portrait that holds boldness, fear, warning and beauty together.
days.context: The observer watches birds around Wick Farm’s garden, fruit bushes and nearby hedges. His attention gradually settles on the blackbird.
days.contentNote: Hunting is mentioned as one setting in which birds give alarm. The author’s comparisons to princes, national character and thieves are personification, not scientific descriptions.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Eight; complete source paragraphs 306–314 in the accompanying source index; opens “Among the most constant residents in the garden at Wick Farm are the”; closes “two or three there after the worms and caterpillars, and so forth.”.

questions.prompt: How does the blackbird’s approach to the garden differ from the thrush’s?
facilitatorNotes: The thrush advances gradually under cover, while the blackbird waits and makes a sudden rush. The comparison prepares the blackbird’s mixture of boldness and alarm.
evidence: he makes a desperate rush for the fruit trees or the lawn.

questions.prompt: What makes the blackbird a “general sentinel” rather than merely a noisy neighbour?
facilitatorNotes: Its alarm changes the behaviour of several kinds of birds and rabbits. Locate the chain of responses; the warning can protect other creatures as well as the caller.
evidence: immediately away goes pigeon or woodpecker, thrushes fly further down the hedge, and the rabbits feeding in the grass lift up their heads

questions.prompt: How does the leisurely singing complicate the earlier portrait of a hurried fruit-raider?
facilitatorNotes: The song introduces composure and artistic ease alongside the rushed raids. Readers can argue for a more rounded portrait or for the observer’s affection, using the shift in rhythm and comparison.
evidence: He sings in a quiet, leisurely way, as a great artist should—there is no haste

days.title: The Meadow Lark
days.challenge: Notice the move from an actual bird in weather to a broader claim about human responses to difficulty.
days.focus: An admired singer becomes an exception rather than an easy model everyone can follow.
days.context: Dank means damp and chilly. Compare the two closing statements after reading each stanza aloud.

excerpt.locator: The Meadow Lark; complete poem, opening “Though the winds be dank,” and closing “Who sing when skies are gray!”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza give the bird a stance toward thunder?
facilitatorNotes: The bird laughs when thunder mutters, making its song seem a spirited reply to threatening weather.
evidence: And laughs at the thunder when it mutters.

questions.prompt: What does the second stanza admit that simple cheer-up advice might ignore?
facilitatorNotes: Song can become difficult and silence more welcome when the heart is troubled. The poem recognizes limits as well as admiration.
evidence: And silence than song by far seems sweeter.

questions.prompt: How is the final few different from the earlier happy bird?
facilitatorNotes: The focus widens from one creature to rarity among travelers through life. It honors resilience without claiming it is effortless or universal.
evidence: Oh, few are they along the way

days.title: Kaa’s Hunting — Lessons and an omission
days.challenge: Separate the value of a lesson from the teacher’s methods.
days.focus: A gap in instruction becomes important when a child seeks kindness elsewhere.
days.context: This story returns to Mowgli’s younger years, before his departure from the pack. Baloo teaches words that let him ask other jungle creatures for protection.
days.contentNote: Baloo strikes and bruises Mowgli; the text’s defense of beating is open to criticism. Its “outcaste” language applies a historical social hierarchy to imaginary animal groups.

excerpt.locator: Kaa’s Hunting — Lessons and an omission; source paragraphs 238–277 in downloaded transcription; opens “ALL that is told here happened some time before Mowgli was turned out of the Seeonee wolf-pack.”; closes “"I--I? How was I to guess he would play with such dirt. The Monkey People! Faugh!"”.

questions.prompt: What limit does the hunting reply place on a stranger’s freedom?
facilitatorNotes: It permits survival while restricting unnecessary killing. The law makes entry into another territory conditional on responsibility.
evidence: Hunt, then, for food, but not for pleasure

questions.prompt: Why does the Monkey People’s invitation appeal to Mowgli beyond the promise of leadership?
facilitatorNotes: He has been hurt and wants affection, play, and recognition. The appeal exposes a consequence of Baloo’s harsh teaching.
evidence: They do not hit me with hard paws

questions.prompt: How does Bagheera’s final criticism complicate the idea that Mowgli alone is at fault?
facilitatorNotes: The teacher omitted a danger because he assumed the child would avoid it. Knowledge that adults take for granted may need explanation.
evidence: Baloo should have warned thee against them

days.title: Kaa’s Hunting — Taken through the trees
days.challenge: Track how a frightened character moves from feeling to planning.
days.focus: Different kinds of movement and knowledge make different kinds of help possible.
days.context: The Monkey People want Mowgli to teach them to build shelters. They seize him while he sleeps beside Baloo and Bagheera.
days.contentNote: Includes abduction, animal violence, and Baloo’s distressed wishes for punishment of himself. The narrator’s sweeping claims about the monkeys belong to a satirical fantasy.

excerpt.locator: Kaa’s Hunting — Taken through the trees; source paragraphs 278–304 in downloaded transcription; opens “A fresh shower came down on their heads, and the two trotted away, taking Mowgli with them. Wha”; closes “s faded brown shoulder against the panther, and they went off to look for Kaa, the Rock Python.”.

questions.prompt: How do the monkeys turn Bagheera’s angry pursuit into a flattering story about themselves?
facilitatorNotes: They confuse attention with admiration, ignoring why he is pursuing them. Their claim exposes their hunger for recognition.
evidence: He has noticed us!

questions.prompt: Why is sending Rann a message more useful than struggling against the carriers?
facilitatorNotes: Mowgli cannot safely escape in the treetops. A bird can follow from above and bring information to rescuers who have fallen behind.
evidence: Mark my trail!

questions.prompt: How does recalling “To each his own fear” help Baloo replace panic with a plan?
facilitatorNotes: The monkeys do not fear the bear or panther in the branches, but fear the climbing python. Baloo identifies help suited to this specific problem.
evidence: To each his own fear

days.title: Kaa’s Hunting — Recruiting an ally
days.challenge: Distinguish several motives that can produce cooperation.
days.focus: Flattery, wounded pride, love, and shared rules all enter a rescue.
days.context: Baloo and Bagheera seek the python Kaa, whom the monkeys fear. They must persuade him to help and discover where Mowgli has been taken.
days.contentNote: Includes threats of predation. Kaa’s traits are fictionalized; this is not a guide to approaching or handling snakes.

excerpt.locator: Kaa’s Hunting — Recruiting an ally; source paragraphs 305–337 in downloaded transcription; opens “They found him stretched out on a warm ledge in the afternoon sun, admiring his beautiful new c”; closes “one so young remembering the Master Word for the birds while he was being pulled across trees!"”.

questions.prompt: What is Bagheera doing when he repeats the monkeys’ supposed insult almost casually?
facilitatorNotes: He provokes Kaa’s pride while pretending merely to recall words. His tact makes a request for help feel like Kaa’s own quarrel.
evidence: as though he were trying to remember something

questions.prompt: How does Baloo’s broken sentence change the tone of his praise of Mowgli?
facilitatorNotes: He moves from boasting about a famous pupil to admitting personal attachment. The hesitation exposes what matters beneath his teacher’s pride.
evidence: I--we--love him

questions.prompt: Why does Rann treat his help as an obligation rather than an exceptional favor?
facilitatorNotes: Mowgli used a recognized appeal that establishes kinship and protection. The lesson works because other creatures honor the shared rule.
evidence: The boy held the Master Word

days.title: To the Clouds
days.challenge: Navigate a long sentence sequence that moves from visual observation toward a wish to see beyond what is visible.
days.focus: Clouds become moving images and a screen between human curiosity and divine mystery.
days.context: Gauze suggests thin fabric. The poem’s religious interpretation belongs to its speaker; discuss how the visible descriptions support the final wish.
days.contentNote: Contains Christian religious imagery and a speaker’s imagined vision of the Creator.

excerpt.locator: To the Clouds; complete poem, opening “O painted clouds! sweet beauties of the sky,” and closing “And view the dwelling of all majesty.”.

questions.prompt: How do the hunter and black-water comparisons produce different kinds of motion?
facilitatorNotes: Fleet hunters suggest speed, while deep black waters suggest weight and slow menace. The speaker admires contrasting cloud states.
evidence: Like black deep waters slowly moving by,

questions.prompt: Which cloud scene produces the calmest response, and how is it described?
facilitatorNotes: The evening clouds are compared with an uncurved, smooth pool, matching the soul’s placid gaze.
evidence: Still as the even-pool, uncurv’d and smooth,

questions.prompt: How does the final wish change clouds from objects to a barrier?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker wants to wipe away sky-coverings and glimpse their divine source. The wish goes beyond what observation can establish.
evidence: To catch a glimpse of Him who bids you reign,

days.title: Banners above the Sierra — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect the physical explanation of drifting snow with the later description of a particular view.
days.focus: The interaction of moving particles, sunlight and viewpoint in a seemingly solid banner.
days.context: A snow-banner is windblown snow streaming from an exposed mountain summit. Muir first explains its material, then recalls seeing a remarkable display from Yosemite in 1873.
days.contentNote: Muir describes travelling through avalanche snow during a gale.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Snow-Banners; complete source paragraphs 68–70 in the accompanying source index; opens “The most magnificent storm phenomenon I ever saw, surpassing in showy grandeur”; closes “leaving only the black peaks, the white banners, and the blue sky.”.

questions.prompt: What prepares snow crystals to become the material of a banner?
facilitatorNotes: Collisions and repeated rolling wear their angles away into loose dust, which an upward wind can lift. Trace both preparation and transport.
evidence: the whole mass is reduced to dust.

questions.prompt: Why does Muir abandon the ice-cone investigation he first intended?
facilitatorNotes: The storm briefly exposes the cone, but the unexpected banners demand a wider and higher viewpoint. The episode shows observation changing an investigator’s immediate plan.
evidence: I at once let the ice-cone go

questions.prompt: What makes these banners look like cloth, and what reveals that they are not solid cloth?
facilitatorNotes: Silky texture, regular attachment and streamers resemble fabric; fading translucent ends and light from countless particles disclose snow in motion. Different details support the two impressions.
evidence: how dense and opaque they are at the point of attachment, and how filmy and translucent toward the end

days.title: Kaa’s Hunting — The city of boasts
days.challenge: Compare impressive surroundings and declarations with practical conduct.
days.focus: An elaborate setting cannot supply the cooperation its occupants lack.
days.context: Rann has located Mowgli in an abandoned city. Bagheera and Kaa hurry there while the Monkey People celebrate their captive.
days.contentNote: Includes captivity, pinching, threatened beating, and a stigmatizing use of “madness.” The city and animal society are imagined.

excerpt.locator: Kaa’s Hunting — The city of boasts; source paragraphs 338–363 in downloaded transcription; opens “"It was most firmly driven into him," said Bagheera. "But I am proud of him, and now we must go”; closes “ ruined of any, and the big snake was delayed a while before he could find a way up the stones.”.

questions.prompt: What does the honeycomb comparison make us notice about the ruined houses?
facilitatorNotes: Their repeated chambers remain, but the organized life once filling them is absent. The image combines pattern with emptiness.
evidence: empty honeycombs filled with blackness

questions.prompt: Why is the phrase about making Mowgli grateful especially revealing?
facilitatorNotes: The monkeys use force while claiming he is happy. Their actions directly contradict the generous picture they present of themselves.
evidence: pinching him to make him grateful

questions.prompt: What is missing from the monkeys’ proof that they are wonderful?
facilitatorNotes: Agreement is treated as evidence. Their failure to feed a guest or learn the promised skill supplies contrary evidence the chorus ignores.
evidence: We all say so, and so it must be true

days.title: Kaa’s Hunting — A rescue needs rescuers
days.challenge: Follow how help moves in more than one direction.
days.focus: Strength works with knowledge, communication, and the courage to ask for aid.
days.context: Bagheera reaches the terrace where Mowgli is held. Baloo and Kaa approach separately, and the monkeys greatly outnumber them.
days.contentNote: A prolonged animal battle includes injuries and deaths. Kipling’s account of how pythons fight is fantasy, not natural history.

excerpt.locator: Kaa’s Hunting — A rescue needs rescuers; source paragraphs 364–396 in downloaded transcription; opens “The cloud hid the moon, and as Mowgli wondered what would come next he heard Bagheera's light f”; closes “"I take my life from thee, to-night. My kill shall be thy kill if ever thou art hungry, O Kaa."”.

questions.prompt: How does the cobras’ answer reverse our first expectation of the summer-house?
facilitatorNotes: The supposed trap becomes a protected space after Mowgli uses their call. The snakes ask him to protect their young as well.
evidence: Stand still, Little Brother, lest thy feet do us harm

questions.prompt: How does Mowgli contribute to his own rescue while still trapped?
facilitatorNotes: He directs Bagheera toward water, which the monkeys cannot follow him into. Observation and speech help where physical escape is impossible.
evidence: To the tank, Bagheera!

questions.prompt: Why does Bagheera hesitate to admit calling Kaa?
facilitatorNotes: He is proud of being a powerful helper and embarrassed by dependence. The scene shows that even the rescuer needs rescue.
evidence: I--I may have cried out in the battle

days.title: Kaa’s Hunting — The way home
days.challenge: Consider the difference between an intention, a consequence, and a fair response.
days.focus: The conclusion combines gratitude, uneasy power, blame, and restored affection.
days.context: Kaa has freed Mowgli and ended the battle. The boy thanks him while the exhausted bear and panther prepare to leave.
days.contentNote: The ending implies predation and explicitly describes a severe beating of a seven-year-old. The narrator approves this punishment; readers may critically examine that approval.

excerpt.locator: Kaa’s Hunting — The way home; source paragraphs 397–429 in downloaded transcription; opens “"All thanks, Little Brother," said Kaa, though his eyes twinkled. "And what may so bold a hunte”; closes “lept so deeply that he never waked when he was put down by Mother Wolf's side in the home-cave.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mowgli offer the skill of his hands after admitting he cannot kill prey himself?
facilitatorNotes: He makes a realistic offer based on a different strength, such as freeing an animal from a trap. Reciprocity need not mean identical abilities.
evidence: I have some skill in these

questions.prompt: How does Mowgli’s response to the dance differ from his friends’ experience?
facilitatorNotes: He sees ordinary movement while they feel compelled to approach. Because he is unaffected, he can lead them away from danger.
evidence: It is only old Kaa making circles on the dust

questions.prompt: Does the ending establish that Mowgli deserved the beating? Use details to explain your judgment.
facilitatorNotes: The narrator endorses punishment and then renewed affection, but readers can question the fairness: Mowgli had decided to avoid the monkeys before being kidnapped, and adults had failed to warn him. Distinguish the story’s judgment from a supported reader response.
evidence: punishment settles all scores

days.title: “Tiger! Tiger!” — A wolf-child at the village gate
days.challenge: Compare the villagers’ explanations of Mowgli with what the reader already knows about him.
days.focus: A stranger is taken into a family through grief, hope and resemblance, while his old loyalties stay alive.
days.context: This story picks up after “Mowgli’s Brothers.” Driven from the wolf pack after he used fire against the tiger Shere Khan, Mowgli goes down to the villages, having vowed to return with the tiger’s hide. Gray Brother is one of his wolf brothers. “By the Bull that bought me” is Mowgli’s oath, recalling the bull paid for his life at the Council Rock.
days.contentNote: Before the story begins, a tiger has carried off a village couple’s son. The narrator describes an Indian village and its priest from a British colonial viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: “Tiger! Tiger!” — A wolf-child at the village gate; source paragraphs 439–461 in downloaded transcription; opens “NOW we must go back to the last tale but one. When Mowgli left the wolf's cave”; closes “again, I will wait for thee in the bamboos at the edge of the grazing-ground."”.

questions.prompt: The priest calls Mowgli’s scars “the bites of wolves.” Why does the narrator insist that Mowgli would never call them bites?
facilitatorNotes: The marks come from rough play with his wolf brothers, “for he knew what real biting meant.” Outsiders read signs of affection as signs of violence, so the reader knows more than the crowd.
evidence: They are the bites of wolves.
for he knew what real biting meant

questions.prompt: What does the priest gain by announcing, “What the jungle has taken the jungle has restored”?
facilitatorNotes: He knows Messua’s husband is rich, so he flatters the family and claims credit for seeing “so far into the lives of men.” Kipling makes the priest’s motive clear, while Messua’s longing for her lost son is sincere.
evidence: What the jungle has taken the jungle has restored.
forget not to honor the priest who sees so far into the lives of men

questions.prompt: Mowgli decides, “if I am a man, a man I must become.” Judging from his first evening, what does he think becoming a man requires, and what does he hold back?
facilitatorNotes: Language comes first: “I must learn their talk,” and he imitates words perfectly. But he will not sleep under the roof and checks that he could tear his way out; he is learning without yet trusting.
evidence: if I am a man, a man I must become
I must learn their talk

questions.prompt: Gray Brother warns, “And that thou mayest be cast out of another pack.” What has already happened to Mowgli that gives this warning weight?
facilitatorNotes: The wolf pack he grew up in has just rejected him. Gray Brother’s comparison of men’s talk to “frogs in a pond” predicts that human crowds may be just as changeable, which readers can test as the story goes on.
evidence: And that thou mayest be cast out of another pack.
their talk is like the talk of frogs in a pond

days.title: “Tiger! Tiger!” — Herd-boy and storyteller
days.challenge: Weigh different kinds of knowledge: Buldeo’s stories, the elders’ agreement and Mowgli’s direct experience.
days.focus: Mowgli’s honesty about the jungle makes him useful to the village and unwelcome at the same time.
days.context: Mowgli has lived for three months in the house of Messua, the woman who believes he may be her lost son. A Tower musket is an old army flintlock; huqas are water-pipes; Khanhiwara is the market town. The bracketed dollar figure after the reward is a note printed in this American edition.
