days.contentNote: Includes the narrator’s colonial-era account of caste and village religion, and Mowgli’s anger at children who tease him, described in a violent image he does not act on.

excerpt.locator: “Tiger! Tiger!” — Herd-boy and storyteller; source paragraphs 462–480 in downloaded transcription; opens “For three months after that night Mowgli hardly ever left the village gate, he”; closes “by the Waingunga, Mowgli would have heard him in those long still mornings.”.

questions.prompt: Which village customs annoy Mowgli most, and what keeps him from losing his temper with the children who mock him?
facilitatorNotes: Clothes, money and ploughing make little sense to him. “The Law of the Jungle had taught him to keep his temper,” because in the jungle survival depends on it; Kipling adds a joke about it being unsportsmanlike to hurt cubs.
evidence: the Law of the Jungle had taught him to keep his temper

questions.prompt: Why is helping the potter’s donkey “very shocking” to the village, and what does Mowgli’s reply to the priest show?
facilitatorNotes: Mowgli helps whoever needs help because he has “not the faintest idea” of caste rank; the village sees a breach of rules. Threatening to put the priest on the donkey shows he respects need, not status. The narrator’s amused tone about caste reflects a British colonial outlook, which students can notice.
evidence: Mowgli had not the faintest idea of the difference that caste makes between man and man
Mowgli threatened to put him on the donkey, too

questions.prompt: How does Mowgli use the ghost-tiger story to challenge everything Buldeo says?
facilitatorNotes: He corrects a fact anyone can check—the tiger “was born lame”—and argues that if Buldeo is wrong about the jungle at his door, his tales of ghosts and gods cannot be trusted. The graybeards’ “True, true” shows agreement based on authority, not evidence.
evidence: That tiger limps because he was born lame, as every one knows.
How, then, shall I believe the tales of ghosts and gods and goblins which he says he has seen?

questions.prompt: The long description of herding says “the day seems longer than most people’s whole lives.” Why slow the story down here, when Shere Khan has sworn to kill Mowgli?
facilitatorNotes: The calm routine and the daily signal from Gray Brother build suspense, because readers know the peace cannot last. The kites that drop at any death quietly foreshadow what is coming.
evidence: the day seems longer than most people's whole lives
that kite would sweep down

days.title: “Tiger! Tiger!” — The trap in the ravine
days.challenge: Follow a plan step by step, using the ravine’s shape and the animals’ behaviour to explain why it works.
days.focus: Mowgli wins through knowledge of habits and ground rather than strength, and the climax is told through the herd.
days.context: Each day Mowgli herds the village buffaloes and looks for Gray Brother on a signal rock: the wolf waits in a ravine only if Shere Khan has returned. Tabaqui is the jackal who serves the tiger; Akela is the old wolf who once led the pack; Rama is the great herd bull.
days.contentNote: A jackal is killed offstage, and the tiger is trampled to death by the buffalo herd; Mowgli then begins to skin it.

excerpt.locator: “Tiger! Tiger!” — The trap in the ravine; source paragraphs 482–514 in downloaded transcription; opens “At last a day came when he did not see Gray Brother at the signal place, and he”; closes “wolves lolled out their tongues, or came forward and tugged as he ordered them.”.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter so much that Shere Khan “killed at dawn” and “has drunk too”?
facilitatorNotes: A tiger heavy with food and water will be sleepy and unable to fight or climb out of the ravine. Mowgli also reads a weakness of character: Shere Khan “could never fast even for the sake of revenge.”
evidence: He killed at dawn,--a pig,--and he has drunk too.
Shere Khan could never fast even for the sake of revenge

questions.prompt: Explain Mowgli’s plan in your own words. Why does he split the herd into bulls and cows?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to “catch Shere Khan between the bulls and the cows.” The cows guarding calves are the more dangerous group, so they block the lower end, while the bulls charge down from the head of the ravine. Students should use the steep sides that give a tiger no foothold.
evidence: catch Shere Khan between the bulls and the cows
they had no calves to protect

questions.prompt: Surprise might seem safer. Why does Mowgli shout down the ravine and call Shere Khan “Cattle-thief” before the charge?
facilitatorNotes: He wants the tiger to know who has beaten him—“I must tell Shere Khan who comes”—and he summons him “to the Council Rock,” echoing the vow he made there. With the trap set, the shout costs him little.
evidence: I must tell Shere Khan who comes.
Cattle-thief, it is time to come to the Council Rock!

questions.prompt: Mowgli calls the tiger’s end “a dog’s death.” What does he mean, and does it change how you judge his victory?
facilitatorNotes: Shere Khan died running, without fighting—“he would never have shown fight.” Some readers think a bully’s inglorious end is fitting; others notice that Mowgli won by a trick rather than courage in combat. Both readings can use the evidence.
evidence: Brothers, that was a dog's death
But he would never have shown fight.

days.title: “Tiger! Tiger!” — Cast out twice
days.challenge: Compare two rejections—by the wolf pack earlier and by the village now—and the reasons each group gives.
days.focus: Keeping a promise costs Mowgli a home, and the story ends with belonging defined by chosen loyalty.
days.context: Shere Khan lies dead in the ravine, and Mowgli is skinning him with the wolves’ help. A rupee is a coin and an anna a small fraction of one; Buldeo is the village hunter. The song Mowgli makes up on the hide is printed after the story and is not included here.
days.contentNote: Villagers throw stones and fire a musket at Mowgli, wounding a buffalo; the tiger’s hide is pegged out at the wolves’ council. The narrator’s remarks about “native hunters” and sorcery reflect a colonial viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: “Tiger! Tiger!” — Cast out twice; source paragraphs 515–559 in downloaded transcription; opens “Presently a hand fell on his shoulder, and looking up he saw Buldeo with the”; closes “But that is a story for grown-ups.”.

questions.prompt: How does Buldeo’s attitude change between “What is this folly?” and “Maharaj! Great King”?
facilitatorNotes: He begins with contempt and greed for the reward, then, pinned by a wolf that obeys a boy, decides Mowgli is a sorcerer and grovels. Mowgli’s mild reply shows he has no interest in revenge on the old man.
evidence: What is this folly?
Maharaj! Great King

questions.prompt: Mowgli says, “Last time it was because I was a man. This time it is because I am a wolf.” What does this reveal about the two groups that have cast him out?
facilitatorNotes: Each group rejects him for being different from itself, whichever difference is handy. Akela makes the same point: “They are not unlike the Pack, these brothers of thine.”
evidence: Last time it was because I was a man. This time it is because I am a wolf.
They are not unlike the Pack, these brothers of thine

questions.prompt: Why does Mowgli spare the village after it stones him?
facilitatorNotes: One person’s kindness outweighs the crowd’s cruelty: “we will not hurt the village, for Messua was kind to me.” His restraint contrasts with the mob and shows the loyalty he learned in the jungle.
evidence: No; we will not hurt the village, for Messua was kind to me.
thank Messua that I do not come in with my wolves

questions.prompt: When the wolves beg to be led again, Bagheera answers, “Ye fought for freedom, and it is yours. Eat it, O Wolves.” What is he saying about freedom, and what does Mowgli choose instead?
facilitatorNotes: Bagheera mocks the pack: they wanted freedom from the Law and must now live with the lawlessness it brought. Mowgli chooses to hunt with the four cubs who choose him—belonging by loyalty rather than by membership.
evidence: Ye fought for freedom, and it is yours. Eat it, O Wolves.
And we will hunt with thee

days.title: Martins test a stone wall — excerpt
days.challenge: Separate a directly witnessed failure from increasingly extended hypotheses about migration and group life.
days.focus: How an unsuccessful nesting attempt becomes an argument against infallible instinct.
days.context: Sand martins usually excavate nest holes in sandy banks. Jefferies watches a group try the old mortar of an orchard wall instead.
days.contentNote: The passage describes boys taking martins’ nests and refers to the shooting of young rooks, rural practices of the 1870s.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Nine; complete source paragraphs 319–324 in the accompanying source index; opens “Broad green paths, wide enough for three or four to walk abreast,”; closes “we suppose that it is reserved to a certain bird to give the signal.”.

questions.prompt: What evidence suggests that hard mortar, rather than fear of people, makes the martins leave?
facilitatorNotes: The birds persist while people stop to watch, but their holes remain shallow and the mortar grows harder beneath the surface. Their departure follows unsuccessful work.
evidence: the birds did not seem in the least alarmed, and evidently only left because they found the wall impenetrable.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the explanation about young martins are assumed rather than established?
facilitatorNotes: He supposes they are displaced young birds lacking experience; he has not identified their ages or watched their departure from a quarry. “If” and “I imagine” should remain attached to the claim.
evidence: if young birds, as we have supposed them to be

questions.prompt: Why does the passage turn from nest building to collective defence and leadership?
facilitatorNotes: These comparisons explore advantages and coordination of group life: numbers can deter a hawk, while a signal may explain simultaneous departure. The observed wall episode supports questions, but not every proposed social explanation is demonstrated.
evidence: The comparative safety afforded by numbers is perhaps a reason why many species of birds are gregarious.

days.title: Sunset
days.challenge: Follow the changing light and sound while distinguishing observed evening from the speaker’s emotional interpretation.
days.focus: Personified sky and river make the close of day seem ceremonial and mournful.
days.context: Lay means song. The dying day is a familiar personification of sunset, not a person’s death.

excerpt.locator: Sunset; complete poem, opening “The river sleeps beneath the sky,” and closing “And shakes her mantle darkly down.”.

questions.prompt: How does the sleeping river holding shadows shape the opening mood?
facilitatorNotes: The river seems quiet and protective, creating rest before the explicitly mournful language arrives.
evidence: And clasps the shadows to its breast;

questions.prompt: What makes the first star seem to participate in a conversation across the sky?
facilitatorNotes: It lifts a face and twinkles toward the moon, turning points of light into responsive figures.
evidence: And twinkles to the moon afar

questions.prompt: Does the poem prove that the lark mourns, or reveal the speaker’s feeling?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase with me shows emotion projected onto the silencing bird. A reader may hear sadness, dignified closure, or peaceful rest if the details support it.
evidence: And mourns with me the dying day.

days.title: The Eagle (fragment)
days.challenge: Slow down six lines to trace scale, motion, and the sudden switch from still observation to descent.
days.focus: Verbs and an unexpected sea-image make a compact scene forceful.
days.context: This is the complete six-line poem published with the label fragment, not an excerpt cut by this collection. Azure means blue.

excerpt.locator: The Eagle (fragment); complete poem, opening “He clasps the crag with hooked hands;” and closing “And like a thunderbolt he falls.”.

questions.prompt: What happens when the eagle’s claws are called hooked hands?
facilitatorNotes: The human term makes gripping feel purposeful and strong, while hooked preserves the animal shape.
evidence: He clasps the crag with hooked hands;

questions.prompt: Why might the sea appear wrinkled and crawling from the eagle’s position?
facilitatorNotes: Height compresses waves into distant texture and makes motion seem slow. The description indirectly establishes the observer’s elevation.
evidence: The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls;

questions.prompt: How does the thunderbolt comparison change the pace of the ending?
facilitatorNotes: After gripping, standing, and watching, the sudden fall concentrates power into one rapid motion. The poem does not specify prey or outcome, so do not invent them.
evidence: And like a thunderbolt he falls.

days.title: Cranford, chapter III — An old acquaintance
days.challenge: Mark the difference between reported fact, a speaker’s guess, and the narrator’s romantic expectations.
days.focus: Indirect evidence gives an emotional history without granting the reader complete certainty.
days.context: After Miss Jenkyns’s death, Mary stays with the younger sister, Miss Matty. Miss Pole tells Mary about Thomas Holbrook, once a suitor.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter III — An old acquaintance; source paragraphs 138–153 in downloaded transcription; opens “And _now_ I come to the love affair.”; closes “d never came back till our early tea-time, when I thought she looked as if she had been crying.”.

questions.prompt: How does Miss Pole’s qualification change what we can claim about the failed courtship?
facilitatorNotes: A proposal and refusal are reported, but the sister’s role remains speculation; readers should not turn that inference into certainty.
evidence: it is only a guess of mine

questions.prompt: What does Mary’s image of her imagined castle being blown up reveal about her as well as about Holbrook’s age?
facilitatorNotes: Mary has invented a romance too quickly; the comic explosion exposes her own assumptions about love and age.
evidence: blowing up my castle

questions.prompt: Why does the unfinished shopping matter more than an explicit declaration of feeling?
facilitatorNotes: Both people become distracted by the reunion. Their abandoned errands make the emotional disturbance visible.
evidence: not having purchased either green or red silk

days.title: Cranford, chapter IV — Dinner at Woodley
days.challenge: Compare different characters’ responses to the same house, books, and table manners.
days.focus: Hospitality and pleasure put pressure on rules about what is proper.
days.context: Mr Holbrook invites Miss Matty, Miss Pole, and Mary to his country home. Matty once wished to marry him.
days.contentNote: Smoking and class-bound etiquette appear as historical customs.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter IV — Dinner at Woodley; source paragraphs 156–178 in downloaded transcription; opens “A FEW days after, a note came from Mr Holbrook, asking us—impartially asking both of us—in a fo”; closes “o hard a word. I should call him eccentric; very clever people always are!” replied Miss Matty.”.

questions.prompt: How does the counting-house challenge a view of reading as a badge of social standing?
facilitatorNotes: Its disordered books reflect pleasure and use, rather than a display of approved authors or elegant furniture.
evidence: He evidently chose his books in accordance with his own tastes

questions.prompt: Why does Mary describe eating peas with a knife as though it were a dangerous adventure?
facilitatorNotes: The mock-heroic rhythm shows how large tiny breaches of etiquette feel in Cranford, while proving the danger imaginary.
evidence: I saw, I imitated, I survived!

questions.prompt: How do Matty and Miss Pole judge the same unconventional habits differently?
facilitatorNotes: Matty’s affection produces a generous label, while Miss Pole emphasizes uncouthness; each word reveals its speaker’s position.
evidence: I should call him eccentric

days.title: Cranford, chapter IV — Learning to notice ash-buds
days.challenge: Read dialogue for the gap between genuine attention and polite performance.
days.focus: Poetry sharpens one person’s observation while becoming background sound for others.
days.context: After dinner, Mary walks with Holbrook, who quotes poems as he observes the countryside.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter IV — Learning to notice ash-buds; source paragraphs 180–199 in downloaded transcription; opens “When Mr Holbrook returned, he proposed a walk in the fields; but the two elder ladies were afra”; closes “y before her this day, and she was annoyed at finding that golden time so far away in the past.”.

questions.prompt: What has poetry taught Holbrook that a lifetime in the country had not?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase directs his attention to an overlooked color; literature changes how he sees familiar surroundings.
evidence: Black as ash-buds in March

questions.prompt: How does Miss Pole’s explanation alter Mary’s account of the poetry reading?
facilitatorNotes: Mary imagines literary admiration, while Miss Pole wants silence for counting; the disclosure corrects the narrator’s inference.
evidence: she had got to a difficult part of her crochet

questions.prompt: Why does Martha’s well-meant concern hurt Matty particularly on this evening?
facilitatorNotes: The visit has revived her younger self and old hopes; a reminder of age clashes with that inward experience.
evidence: Martha, I’m not yet fifty-two!

days.title: A Farewell
days.challenge: Listen for permanence in the repeated refrain and distinguish continuing nature from a departing observer.
days.focus: Small changes in recurring sentences make a farewell increasingly final.
days.context: A rivulet is a small stream and lea means meadow. The poem does not explain why the speaker is leaving.
days.contentNote: A farewell with a sense of permanent absence; the reason for departure is unstated.

excerpt.locator: A Farewell; complete poem, opening “Flow down, cold rivulet, to the sea,” and closing “For ever and for ever.”.

questions.prompt: How does rivulet then river alter the scale of the farewell?
facilitatorNotes: The stream’s continuing journey grows beyond the local place where the speaker walked, contrasting with the speaker’s absence.
evidence: A rivulet then a river:

questions.prompt: What remains after the speaker’s footsteps cease?
facilitatorNotes: Trees, bees, sunlight, and moonlight continue. The repeated here fixes an enduring place despite the personal departure.
evidence: And here by thee will hum the bee,

questions.prompt: Can forever sound both consoling and painful in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: Nature’s continuity may comfort, while the speaker’s repeated exclusion makes it painful. Either emphasis should account for both continuing flow and absent footsteps.
evidence: But not by thee my steps shall be,

days.title: Village work and changing industry — excerpt
days.challenge: Keep track of several crafts, then compare the different ways machinery and larger workshops affect them.
days.focus: The distinction between a trade disappearing and a craftsperson adapting.
days.context: The stream below the chalk hills supports willows used by local makers. Jefferies moves through the village’s workshops and considers changes visible in their work.
days.contentNote: The author uses class judgments and describes workers as “human machines.” Discuss these as his social perspective, not a neutral description of people.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Four; complete source paragraphs 130–137 in the accompanying source index; opens “In the meadows of the vale the waters of the same stream irrigate”; closes “many of which may be found in far distant towers ringing to this day.”.

questions.prompt: How does the blacksmith’s experience differ from that of the willow and hurdle makers?
facilitatorNotes: New machinery increases the blacksmith’s work and prompts new learning; straw weaving and larger producers reduce the other village businesses. The passage does not show technology having one uniform effect.
evidence: they have learned a good deal, though some of the pieces still have to be replaced from the implement factories if broken.

questions.prompt: Why do some customers still choose the village cobbler despite cheaper machine-sewn boots?
facilitatorNotes: The cobbler knows the demands of wet fields and reinforces boots for local use. His knowledge supports his trade, although the comic delay complicates the praise.
evidence: understands what is wanted better than the artisan of the cities

questions.prompt: Why does moving a workshop into the countryside not necessarily reverse “centralisation” in this account?
facilitatorNotes: Location is not the only issue: owners can retain city offices while employees do the work elsewhere. Jefferies contrasts wage labour with making and selling one’s own product.
evidence: they do not labour for their own hands in their own little shops at home

days.title: Cranford, chapter IV — A book and a silence
days.challenge: Build a cautious inference from small actions, reports, and withheld speech.
days.focus: The narrator balances concern with respect for an intensely private grief.
days.context: After the visit to Woodley, Matty waits for Holbrook to call. Mary notices clues that Matty does not explain.
days.contentNote: A loved person becomes gravely ill; the conversation includes period stereotypes about Paris.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter IV — A book and a silence; source paragraphs 200–224 in downloaded transcription; opens “But she never spoke of any former and more intimate acquaintance with Mr Holbrook. She had prob”; closes “of Mr Holbrook. So we talked softly and quietly of old times through the long November evening.”.

questions.prompt: How do the cap and the seat by the window express something Matty never directly says?
facilitatorNotes: They suggest anticipation of a visitor and a wish to be seen at her best; the inference rests on a pattern of actions.
evidence: her best cap every day

questions.prompt: What does Martha’s complaint reveal about her trustworthiness as well as her frustration?
facilitatorNotes: She wants to see Jem but keeps her promise even when she could hide a visit. Her bluntness coexists with loyalty.
evidence: I’ve given my word, and I’ll stick to it

questions.prompt: Why does Mary refrain from telling Miss Pole what she has inferred?
facilitatorNotes: Understanding another person does not confer a right to expose her; Mary recognizes the difference between sympathy and intrusion.
evidence: I felt almost guilty

days.title: Cranford, chapter IV — What grief changes
days.challenge: Notice how an unspoken loss becomes a change in someone else’s opportunities.
days.focus: Grief is conveyed through objects and a revised household rule rather than a confession.
days.context: News arrives that Holbrook has died. Matty has not openly discussed her old attachment to him.
days.contentNote: The passage concerns bereavement and the loss of a former love.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter IV — What grief changes; source paragraphs 225–237 in downloaded transcription; opens “The next day Miss Pole brought us word that Mr Holbrook was dead. Miss Matty heard the news in ”; closes “Though Miss Matty was startled, she submitted to Fate and Love.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the location of the book strong evidence despite Matty’s silence?
facilitatorNotes: Keeping it beside a cherished daily book suggests lasting value; the object preserves an attachment she does not voice.
evidence: the book he gave her lies with her Bible

questions.prompt: What does Matty’s correction “not widows’, of course” allow the reader to understand about her mourning?
facilitatorNotes: Matty wishes to mourn a relationship without claiming a public status she never had; the wording expresses both grief and restraint.
evidence: not widows’, of course

questions.prompt: How does Matty’s revised rule for Martha answer her own history?
facilitatorNotes: She allows a respectful courtship rather than repeating a restriction that may have cost her happiness.
evidence: that I should grieve any young hearts

days.title: The Nightingale’s Nest
days.challenge: Follow the speaker’s directions and interruptions, then evaluate the tension between curiosity and protecting the bird.
days.focus: Detailed observation leads to an ethical decision, while the poem also exposes the observer’s intrusion.
days.context: The companion is addressed as if walking beside the speaker. Read the search as a sequence of decisions; the poem need not be treated as a guide to approaching nests.
days.contentNote: A nesting bird is frightened by observers; eggs are left in place.

excerpt.locator: The Nightingale’s Nest; complete poem, opening “Up this green woodland-ride let’s softly rove,” and closing “As the old woodland’s legacy of song.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the bird’s plain dress surprise the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: Its celebrated music seems to promise visual magnificence, yet it is russet brown. The contrast questions a link between beauty of song and showy appearance.
evidence: Should have no better dress than russet brown.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker recognize that the visitors have changed the bird’s behavior?
facilitatorNotes: The bird stops singing and shows fear; the speaker explicitly admits that their presence delays its joys.
evidence:
our presence doth retard
Her joys,

questions.prompt: Does leaving the nest untouched fully remove the tension in the search?
facilitatorNotes: It protects the eggs from removal, yet trampling branches and provoking fear have already intruded. Accept praise for restraint or criticism of intrusion when grounded in both stages.
evidence: So here we’ll leave them, still unknown to wrong,

days.title: A hedge becomes a highway — excerpt
days.challenge: Build a mental map from directional prose and compare a busy route with a nearby unused route.
days.focus: How repeated observations turn scattered bird sightings into a pattern of travel.
days.context: The orchard at Wick Farm attracts many kinds of birds. A ha-ha is a recessed boundary that does not interrupt the view; here it separates the orchard from a meadow hedge.
days.contentNote: The opening compares the orchard to an “Eastern” market in the author’s nineteenth-century language. The comparison expresses his viewpoint rather than a comprehensive description of any society.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Nine; complete source paragraphs 331–335 in the accompanying source index; opens “Just as men from various causes congregate in particular places, so”; closes “showing the routes and resorts of furred and feathered creatures.”.

questions.prompt: What physical features make the busy hedge more than a bare line dividing two fields?
facilitatorNotes: It contains varied shrubs, trees, a small stream and a sheltered branching hollow. These details help the reader imagine a connected route with cover, though the author does not prove which feature attracts each bird.
evidence: a hollow space arched over and roofed with boughs

questions.prompt: Why include the parallel hedge where an observer might see only a robin?
facilitatorNotes: It acts as a comparison: proximity to the house alone cannot explain the busy route. The difference strengthens the claim that birds favour particular paths.
evidence: it is comparatively deserted.

questions.prompt: What would have to appear on the map Jefferies imagines at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Trace the first hedge to the orchard, across the wall and road to the second hedge, and onward to the favoured meadow; include the other route beside a brook. A defensible map keeps routes and destinations distinct.
evidence: I think I could make a map of these fields, showing the routes and resorts of furred and feathered creatures.

days.title: Cranford, chapter V — Candles and old letters
days.challenge: Follow a transition from comic habits to a painful encounter with time.
days.focus: Ordinary household objects hold both absurdity and deep emotional value.
days.context: Mary describes small economies before Miss Matty brings out letters written by her parents long ago.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter V — Candles and old letters; source paragraphs 239–243 in downloaded transcription; opens “I HAVE often noticed that almost every one has his own individual small economies—careful habit”; closes “, faded ink; but no, even through her tears, she saw and remembered her little economical ways.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary confess her own hoarding after describing other people’s economies?
facilitatorNotes: She places herself among the people she teases, preventing the humor from becoming merely superior or cruel.
evidence: String is my foible

questions.prompt: How does the candle rotation combine thrift with performance?
facilitatorNotes: They save fuel but preserve the appearance of abundance for an imagined visitor; effort is spent maintaining a social fiction.
evidence: to look as if we burnt two always

questions.prompt: Why might happy old letters make Mary sadder than sorrowful ones?
facilitatorNotes: Their vivid present contrasts with the reader’s knowledge that its people and hopes have passed away.
evidence: I should have felt less melancholy

days.title: Cranford, chapter V — Lives behind the portrait
days.challenge: Compare private language, public image, and later memory across several letter writers.
days.focus: Domestic correspondence reveals people whom a formal portrait and sermon conceal.
days.context: Mary and Matty read family letters before destroying private papers. Paduasoy is a rich silk fabric; trousseau means wedding clothes.
days.contentNote: Includes historical religious language and a reference to hanging in a severe grandfather’s warnings.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter V — Lives behind the portrait; source paragraphs 244–254 in downloaded transcription; opens “The earliest set of letters were two bundles tied together, and ticketed (in Miss Jenkyns’s han”; closes “uded that he had died young, or else surely his name would have been alluded to by his sisters.”.

questions.prompt: How does the young rector’s language challenge Mary’s picture of him?
facilitatorNotes: The stately portrait suggests stiffness, but his intimate letters are eager and direct; a public image captures only one role.
evidence: short homely sentences, right fresh from the heart

questions.prompt: What change in values does the reused white Paduasoy make visible?
facilitatorNotes: The coveted wedding finery becomes something for her child; the same material connects vanity, affection, and continuity.
evidence: a christening cloak for the baby

questions.prompt: How does the wife’s response to classical verses expose a mismatch in the correspondence?
facilitatorNotes: She needs practical household guidance while he performs literary accomplishment; her misspelling does not make her concerns unimportant.
evidence: I thowt to have had a letter about killing the pig

days.title: Cranford, chapter V — The letter that must not burn
days.challenge: Compare polished performance with an urgent, imperfect voice.
days.focus: Writing’s emotional power need not depend on formal correctness.
days.context: Matty prizes her late sister Deborah’s polished letters. Mary finds their elaborate reflections less revealing than ordinary details.
days.contentNote: Includes memories of feared invasion and a child’s distress about his mother’s illness.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter V — The letter that must not burn; source paragraphs 255–262 in downloaded transcription; opens “By-and-by we came to packets of Miss Jenkyns’s letters. These Miss Matty did regret to burn. Sh”; closes “t him in the lurch. But he was too fond of mischief. He could never resist a joke. Poor Peter!””.

questions.prompt: Why is the extra candle a revealing measure of Matty’s admiration?
facilitatorNotes: She breaks a cherished economy for Deborah’s words, showing that the letters have unusual importance to her.
evidence: even lighted the second candle

questions.prompt: How does Matty challenge Deborah’s retrospective account of an invasion alarm?
facilitatorNotes: Calm later judgment minimizes fear that felt real while it happened; Matty restores the experience that polished language obscures.
evidence: they were not at all trivial or trifling at the time

questions.prompt: Why does Peter’s badly written, blotted note receive greater protection than the formally superior letters?
facilitatorNotes: Peter’s plea expresses vulnerable love and fear for his mother. Matty saves its living feeling rather than its technical accomplishment.
evidence: badly-written, badly-sealed, badly-directed, blotted note

days.title: Cranford, chapter VI — Poor Peter’s jokes
days.challenge: Follow a story told by a nervous speaker who interrupts herself, delays and protects her listener.
days.focus: Comic tricks build toward a public humiliation, and Matty’s way of telling shows how carefully a family memory has been guarded.
days.context: Chapter V ended with Miss Matty weeping over a childhood note from her brother Peter. Now she tells Mary the story the family never discusses. A “living” is a paid post as a parish clergyman; the Latin proverb means that even good Bernard does not see everything; “hoaxing” means fooling people with tricks. The Rector is Matty’s father; Deborah is the late Miss Jenkyns.
days.contentNote: Ends with a father seizing his teenage son in front of a crowd and flogging him with a cane.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter VI — Poor Peter’s jokes; source paragraphs 264–276 in downloaded transcription; opens “POOR Peter’s career lay before him rather pleasantly mapped out by kind”; closes “indeed, and before all the people he lifted up his cane and flogged Peter!”.

questions.prompt: Before she reaches the “terrible, sad thing,” Miss Matty sends Martha out, locks the door and says, “We’ll put out the candle, my dear.” What do these preparations tell you about the story she is about to tell?
facilitatorNotes: The story has been kept secret for decades and still feels shameful and dangerous to repeat. Darkness may also make painful telling easier. The ritual builds suspense for Mary and the reader.
evidence: We’ll put out the candle, my dear.
At last there was a terrible, sad thing happened.

questions.prompt: Matty refuses to describe Peter’s other jokes “because they might not shock you as they ought to do.” What does this reveal about her own feelings toward them?
facilitatorNotes: She enjoyed them and still half-enjoys them (“I could laugh to think of some of Peter’s jokes”). She performs the disapproval a rector’s daughter is supposed to feel while her affection shows through.
evidence: because they might not shock you as they ought to do
I could laugh to think of some of Peter’s jokes

questions.prompt: As he comes up the street, the Rector first walks slower so the crowd can admire his rhododendron. How does that detail affect your response to what he sees and does next?
facilitatorNotes: His pride in being admired makes the discovery of public mockery more wounding, and the comic build-up makes the sudden violence more shocking. It may help explain his fury without excusing it. Readers may differ on how much sympathy he deserves.
evidence: he walked slower, that they might have more time to admire

questions.prompt: Peter later said the trick was only “to make something to talk about in the town; he never thought of it as affecting Deborah.” Is not thinking about the consequences a defence?
facilitatorNotes: Peter aimed at the town’s love of gossip, but dressing as his sister with a “baby” invited scandal about an unmarried woman. Students may argue that careless harm is still harm, or that a boy’s thoughtlessness deserved correction rather than public violence. Push for reasons from the text.
evidence: to make something to talk about in the town; he never thought of it as affecting Deborah

days.title: Cranford, chapter VI — The search for Peter
days.challenge: Read gestures and silences—a bow, a long kiss, withered cowslips—as evidence of feelings no one states directly.
days.focus: One harsh act of authority changes a whole family; Gaskell shows its cost through the mother’s search and the father’s tears.
days.context: Matty continues the story she is telling Mary in the dark. After the flogging, Peter walked into the house, where Matty was helping their mother make cowslip wine. Old Clare is the family’s servant; “Molly” is the Rector’s name for his wife.
days.contentNote: The family fears that Peter may have drowned or killed himself; a servant offers to drag the ponds, and Matty’s shock breaks out as laughter and screams.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter VI — The search for Peter; source paragraphs 277–291 in downloaded transcription; opens ““My dear, that boy’s trick, on that sunny day, when all seemed going straight”; closes “not born at the time when this occurrence took place, was the one to open it.”.

questions.prompt: After the flogging Peter asks, “Have you done enough, sir?” and then bows to the crowd. What does he communicate by these two actions?
facilitatorNotes: He refuses to be humiliated: the quiet question and the grand bow turn a public punishment into his own dignified performance. Matty says he looked “like a man, not like a boy,” so the scene also marks the end of his childhood at home.
evidence: Have you done enough, sir?
made them a low bow, as grand and as grave as any gentleman

questions.prompt: Why does Matty remember the cowslip wine so exactly, ending with “There was no making of cowslip wine that year at the rectory—nor, indeed, ever after”?
facilitatorNotes: A small household custom stopped for ever, so it becomes a measurable sign of permanent damage. Smell and taste still make Matty “sick and faint,” which shows the memory is bodily as well as mental.
evidence: There was no making of cowslip wine that year at the rectory—nor, indeed, ever after.
they turn me sick and faint

questions.prompt: Compare the Rector’s message “Tell your mother I have flogged Peter, and that he richly deserved it” with what he says later: “Molly! I did not think all this would happen.” How has he changed, and who leads whom by the end of the day?
facilitatorNotes: He moves from certainty and authority to fear, remorse and dependence; his wife, though terrified herself, takes his hand and leads him. Students may debate whether his remorse redeems him or only shows that he acted without thinking.
evidence: Tell your mother I have flogged Peter, and that he richly deserved it.
I did not think all this would happen.

questions.prompt: The mother’s unopened letter says, “Perhaps he has been too severe, and perhaps I have not been kind enough.” Why does it matter that Mary, “a stranger,” is the first person ever to read it?
facilitatorNotes: The letter never reached Peter, so its forgiveness and self-blame were wasted. Mary becomes the witness to a family’s lost chances, which continues the chapter’s concern with letters that arrive too late or never.
evidence: Perhaps he has been too severe, and perhaps I have not been kind enough
I, a stranger, not born at the time when this occurrence took place, was the one to open it

days.title: Cranford, chapter VI — Too late
days.challenge: Distinguish what Matty knew then from what she understands now, and notice how the chapter returns to the present at its end.
days.focus: Grief accumulates through delays, objects and silence, and the chapter closes by turning memory into hope and comedy.
days.context: Peter ran away to Liverpool and joined a navy warship during the wars with France. A captain’s letter told the parents where he was. “Admiral” is the highest naval rank; the “overland route” was a later, quicker way to send letters to India.
days.contentNote: Describes a mother’s decline and death a year after her son leaves, her laying-out and funeral, and later the father’s death, all told with restraint.

excerpt.locator: Cranford, chapter VI — Too late; source paragraphs 292–318 in downloaded transcription; opens “The captain’s letter summoned the father and mother to Liverpool instantly, if”; closes ““No! kissing”—”.

questions.prompt: What small accidents make the parents “too late” to see Peter before his ship sails?
facilitatorNotes: The captain’s letter was delayed, and the post-horses were all at the races, so they had to drive their own gig. Chance, not anyone’s malice, completes the harm the flogging began; students may notice the pattern of letters that come too late.
evidence: the captain’s letter had been detained somewhere, somehow
all the post-horses at Cranford were gone to the races

questions.prompt: The mother talks cheerfully about Peter becoming an admiral. Whom is she protecting, and what does it cost her?
facilitatorNotes: She shields her husband from guilt about “the flogging which was always in his mind,” but she cries bitterly when alone. Students may compare her with Jessie Brown, who also hid grief to protect someone.
evidence: just to make my father think she was quite glad of what came of that unlucky morning’s work
the bitter, bitter crying she had when she was alone

questions.prompt: Why does the Rector decide about Peter’s Indian shawl, “She shall be buried in it”?
facilitatorNotes: It lets Peter’s gift reach his mother after all and gives Peter “that comfort.” It also answers an old regret of the Rector’s own, since she had wished for such a shawl when she married. One gesture carries both men’s remorse.
evidence: She shall be buried in it
It is just such a shawl as she wished for when she was married

questions.prompt: Matty says she sometimes hears Peter’s step, “but the sound always goes past—and Peter never comes.” How does the comic final exchange, ending “No! kissing,” change the mood of that hope?
facilitatorNotes: The sad, still house is interrupted by Martha’s courtship at the door, so ordinary life breaks into memory. Matty’s shocked propriety returns, which is funny. The noise outside also keeps the possibility of someone arriving alive; some readers will hear it as a hint about Peter.
evidence: but the sound always goes past—and Peter never comes
No! kissing

days.title: Rikki-tikki-tavi — Run and find out
days.challenge: Notice how curiosity meets risks the explorer does not yet understand.
days.focus: A newcomer learns that an inviting place contains a struggle for control.
days.context: A flood carries a young mongoose into an English family’s garden in colonial India. The family helps him recover, and he begins exploring.
days.contentNote: Includes a near-drowning, a bird’s death, and a snake attack. The colonial household is viewed favorably by the narrator; animal conduct and religious references are part of the fiction, not wildlife or cultural instruction.

excerpt.locator: Rikki-tikki-tavi — Run and find out; source paragraphs 694–732 in downloaded transcription; opens “THIS is the story of the great war that Rikki-tikki-tavi fought single-handed, through the bath”; closes “ off to the gravel path near the house, and sat down to think. It was a serious matter for him.”.

questions.prompt: How does Rikki-tikki’s family motto explain both his delight in the house and his mishaps there?
facilitatorNotes: Curiosity makes every object interesting, but he investigates baths, ink, and a cigar without knowing their hazards. The same impulse enables learning and risk.
evidence: Run and find out

questions.prompt: What changes when the narrator reveals Nag’s fear beneath his display?
facilitatorNotes: The cobra’s grand speech becomes a strategy to intimidate a dangerous rival, not proof that he feels secure.
evidence: at the bottom of his cold heart he was afraid

questions.prompt: How does Nag’s question work both as an argument and as a distraction?
facilitatorNotes: It questions Rikki’s distinction between kinds of predation, while giving Nagaina time to approach from behind. Its reasoning and its purpose can be evaluated separately.
evidence: You eat eggs. Why should not I eat birds?

days.title: Rikki-tikki-tavi — A small danger and a quiet warning
days.challenge: Compare the danger characters see with the danger the narrator describes.
days.focus: Size, confidence, and fear do not reliably measure the importance of a threat or a helper.
days.context: Rikki-tikki has escaped an attack by the cobras Nag and Nagaina. Near Teddy, another much smaller snake appears.
days.contentNote: Includes a snake being killed and threatened harm. The narrator’s remarks on snakebite and mongoose behavior belong to the fiction.

excerpt.locator: Rikki-tikki-tavi — A small danger and a quiet warning; source paragraphs 733–751 in downloaded transcription; opens “If you read the old books of natural history, you will find they say that when the mongoose fig”; closes “is crawling into the bath-room sluice. You're right, Chuchundra; I should have talked to Chua."”.

questions.prompt: Why can Karait’s small size make him more dangerous in the story?
facilitatorNotes: It makes people overlook him, while his speed and ability to turn create a difficult opponent. Visibility and size are poor measures of risk.
evidence: he is so small that nobody thinks of him

questions.prompt: Why does Rikki-tikki find the father’s blows at the dead snake puzzling?
facilitatorNotes: He sees the immediate task as already finished; the father is still acting from alarm. The difference shows practical action beside lingering human fear.
evidence: What is the use of that?

questions.prompt: How does the comparison for the scratching noise prepare us for Rikki-tikki’s discovery?
facilitatorNotes: It asks us to imagine extreme quiet and close attention. Chuchundra’s fearful warning turns out to contain useful information.
evidence: as faint as that of a wasp walking on a window-pane

days.title: Rikki-tikki-tavi — The water jar
days.challenge: Follow the reasoning that precedes a rapid physical action.
days.focus: The scene combines fear with patience, calculation, and resolve.
days.context: During his night patrol, Rikki-tikki hears Nag and Nagaina planning to attack the family. Nag enters the bathroom and waits beside a water jar.
days.contentNote: Includes a planned attack on a family, an intense animal fight, and a snake killed with a shotgun. Rikki-tikki fears he will die.

excerpt.locator: Rikki-tikki-tavi — The water jar; source paragraphs 752–764 in downloaded transcription; opens “He stole off to Teddy's bath-room, but there was nothing there, and then to Teddy's mother's ba”; closes “ing himself tenderly to find out whether he really was broken into forty pieces, as he fancied.”.

questions.prompt: How does Nagaina’s reason for the attack complicate her role as an enemy?
facilitatorNotes: She seeks safety and space for her future young, even while planning murder. The motive resembles protection, but the proposed means remain destructive.
evidence: our children will need room and quiet

questions.prompt: What does the very slow approach add to the suspense?
facilitatorNotes: Rikki must delay despite urgency, measuring his movement so the snake will not wake. The careful pace stretches the moment before the leap.
evidence: muscle by muscle

questions.prompt: Why does the jar’s position matter to the outcome of the fight?
facilitatorNotes: It gives Rikki temporary leverage to hold the snake’s head. A small feature of the setting becomes crucial once his plan turns into action.
evidence: one second's purchase

days.title: Rikki-tikki-tavi — A song too soon
days.challenge: Compare praise with practical assistance under changing conditions.
days.focus: Premature certainty can distract from an unfinished danger.
days.context: Nag is dead, but Nagaina and her eggs remain. Rikki-tikki seeks information while Darzee celebrates the apparent victory.
days.contentNote: Includes destruction of snake eggs and young, threats against a child, and a description of a dead snake. The tale invites discussion of how warlike framing shapes sympathy.

excerpt.locator: Rikki-tikki-tavi — A song too soon; source paragraphs 765–792 in downloaded transcription; opens “When morning came he was very stiff, but well pleased with his doings. "Now I have Nagaina to s”; closes “ll his father could do was to whisper, "Sit still, Teddy. You mustn't move. Teddy, keep still."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Rikki-tikki object to praise that accurately describes his achievement?
facilitatorNotes: The danger has changed rather than ended. He needs information and action before celebration.
evidence: Is this the time to sing?

questions.prompt: What connection makes Darzee hesitate about destroying the eggs, and how does the narrator treat his hesitation?
facilitatorNotes: He sees a likeness to his own young. The narrator calls him limited and favors his wife’s practical judgment; readers may still recognize the moral difficulty his comparison raises.
evidence: he didn't think at first that it was fair to kill them

questions.prompt: How does Nagaina’s threat change the family’s position?
facilitatorNotes: It removes the hope that obeying her will secure safety. Their stillness delays action while Rikki needs a new way to distract her.
evidence: If you move I strike, and if you do not move I strike

days.title: Rikki-tikki-tavi — The last egg
days.challenge: Track changes in attention, advantage, and certainty.
days.focus: The rescue depends on a distraction and on help that the opening’s heroic claim can obscure.
days.context: Nagaina threatens Teddy on the veranda. Rikki-tikki arrives carrying the last intact egg from her nest.
days.contentNote: Includes a threatened child, destruction of a snake family, and a final underground fight. The story celebrates the mongoose while allowing readers to examine the costs of its war imagery.

excerpt.locator: Rikki-tikki-tavi — The last egg; source paragraphs 793–816 in downloaded transcription; opens “Then Rikki-tikki came up and cried: "Turn round, Nagaina; turn and fight!"”; closes “th tooth and jump and spring and bite, till never a cobra dared show its head inside the walls.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the egg succeed in moving Nagaina’s attention when the challenge to fight did not?
facilitatorNotes: It touches her protective attachment directly. The instant she turns gives Teddy’s father a chance to pull him clear.
evidence: forgetting everything for the sake of the one egg

questions.prompt: What difference does Darzee’s wife make during the chase?
facilitatorNotes: Her interference slows Nagaina just enough for Rikki to catch her. The supposedly single-handed victory depends on another creature’s timely aid.
evidence: the instant's delay brought Rikki-tikki up to her

questions.prompt: How do Darzee and Rikki-tikki give “It is all over” different meanings?
facilitatorNotes: Darzee assumes the mongoose has died because he cannot see the underground fight; Rikki returns to announce the cobra’s defeat. The repeated phrase exposes an inference made too soon.
evidence: It is all over

days.title: We Wear the Mask
days.challenge: Separate public performance from inward feeling and examine whether concealment can be both protective and costly.
days.focus: The collective voice complicates any easy judgment that a smile discloses happiness.
days.context: The mask is figurative. Read the public-facing lines beside the private address to Christ; the poem leaves the identity and extent of its we open to interpretation.
days.contentNote: Figurative wounded-heart and tortured-soul language describes emotional suffering; includes a Christian prayer.

excerpt.locator: We Wear the Mask; complete poem, opening “We wear the mask that grins and lies,” and closing “We wear the mask!”.

questions.prompt: Why give the mask the actions grins and lies?
facilitatorNotes: The false expression belongs to a socially presented face; personification separates outward behavior from what the wearers feel.
evidence: We wear the mask that grins and lies,

questions.prompt: Does the question about the world being over-wise ask for more sympathy or resist scrutiny?
facilitatorNotes: It can resist intrusive counting of suffering while exposing the need for understanding. Accept tension, but require attention to the command that the world see only the mask.
evidence: In counting all our tears and sighs?

questions.prompt: How does the final stanza change the audience of the speech?
facilitatorNotes: An appeal to Christ permits cries hidden from the world. The public song and private suffering coexist rather than cancel one another.
evidence: We smile, but, O great Christ, our cries

days.title: Can a corncrake throw its voice? — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare explanations for a hidden sound and use a contrasting observation to test one of them.
days.focus: How movement and invisibility can account for an apparent special power.
days.context: Corncrakes call from tall meadow grass, where they are difficult to see. Jefferies examines the local belief that their confusing calls make them ventriloquists.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Eleven; complete source paragraphs 410–415 in the accompanying source index; opens “The grass in the meadow or home-field as it begins to grow tall in”; closes “return again, so that you may always know where to go to hear one.”.

questions.prompt: How can the bird’s route create the impression that its call has come from the wrong place?
facilitatorNotes: It runs quickly and changes direction while concealed; by the time a listener reaches a guessed location it may have moved. The account adds the possible effects of furrows and repeated sound.
evidence: When the sound is made now here, now yonder, as the bird travels swiftly—still out of sight—it must be still more difficult.

questions.prompt: Why does Jefferies bring in starlings and finches?
facilitatorNotes: They offer comparison cases in which an unseen bird also misleads the ear. The shared condition is invisibility, weakening the need to give corncrakes a unique power.
evidence: always provided that they are temporarily invisible.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly tests his movement explanation, and what remains uncertain?
facilitatorNotes: A corncrake calling repeatedly from one fixed place can be located, unlike a moving hidden bird. That contrast supports his explanation, but his wording about sound travelling in furrows is still a proposed mechanism.
evidence: When the crake remains a long time in one place, uttering the call continuously, the illusion disappears

days.title: The Poet
days.challenge: Compare the poet’s intended range with the audience’s narrowed praise, attending to the turn in the final two lines.
days.focus: Recognition can misrepresent an artist by rewarding only a limited kind of work.
days.context: The phrase broken tongue belongs to the poem’s critical portrayal of reception. Dialect is a systematic form of language, not evidence of lower intelligence or artistic worth.
days.contentNote: The final phrase uses a historically demeaning characterization of a language variety within a critique of literary reception.

excerpt.locator: The Poet; complete poem, opening “He sang of life, serenely sweet,” and closing “A jingle in a broken tongue.”.

questions.prompt: What range of feeling is suggested by a deeper note within serenely sweet song?
facilitatorNotes: The art is not uniformly pleasant: the deeper note adds seriousness beneath sweetness.
evidence: With, now and then, a deeper note.

questions.prompt: What difference lies between love being a subject and Love itself being in the lays?
facilitatorNotes: The poem claims the songs embody an experience, not merely name it. This heightens the quality the audience overlooks.
evidence: And Love, itself, was in his lays.

questions.prompt: How does calling the praised work a jingle expose a gap between artist and audience?
facilitatorNotes: Jingle contrasts with the rich earlier songs, suggesting that narrow or superficial praise can diminish the maker. The poem critiques reception rather than requiring contempt for dialect art.
evidence: A jingle in a broken tongue.

days.title: The meadow’s two clocks — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish recurring annual change from the much slower transformation that eventually removes a meadow.
days.focus: How one landscape can renew itself each spring yet still change irreversibly.
days.context: Muir’s hidden glacier meadow, introduced earlier in the year, supports summer flowers and a winding brook. Here he follows it through autumn, deep snow and spring before considering its longer geological future.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, The Glacier Meadows; complete source paragraphs 237–244 in the accompanying source index; opens “The summer life we have been depicting lasts with but little abatement”; closes “the varied conditions already alluded to, forming a series of delightful studies.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Muir call the winter snow flowers rather than simply a covering?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison continues the meadow’s flowering season into winter and makes falling crystals part of a recurring display of form and light.
evidence: snow comes in full flower direct from the dark, frozen sky.

questions.prompt: What evidence makes the apparently “twice dead” spring ground an unreliable sign that life has ended?
facilitatorNotes: The final snow melts, new growing points emerge and birds return. Appearance during thaw is a temporary stage in renewal.
evidence: myriads of growing points push eagerly through the steaming mold

questions.prompt: How does a meadow eventually disappear even without a sudden catastrophe?
facilitatorNotes: Deposited soil raises and dries the surface until meadow species lose their suitable conditions and other plants, eventually forest trees, replace them. This long process differs from the yearly return.
evidence: too dry a soil for the specific meadow-plants

days.title: Song of Summer
days.challenge: Read the crafted speech spelling for sound and humor while tracing how a day of idleness becomes a social world.
days.focus: Leisure is defended through sensory abundance and comic human roles assigned to animals.
days.context: This poem uses literary dialect. Read for voice and rhythm without caricature; unfamiliar spellings can be sounded in context.
days.contentNote: Includes boys swimming without clothes, mentioned briefly and without bodily description; uses historical literary dialect.

excerpt.locator: Song of Summer; complete poem, opening “Dis is gospel weathah sho'--” and closing “An' I 'm a-layin' neah huh!”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker claim is the only right activity for this weather?
facilitatorNotes: Dreaming replaces work as the day’s appropriate action; the exaggerated rule establishes playful resistance to duty.
evidence: Nothin' 's right but dreamin'.

questions.prompt: Why make crows a camp meeting and a jaybird a grammar teacher?
facilitatorNotes: The animal sounds become a comic gathering of human activities, so apparent idleness is full of attentive noticing.
evidence: Tryin' to teach him grammah.

questions.prompt: How does summer on a throne explain the final request to be left alone?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker chooses closeness to a reigning season rather than human demands. The image celebrates leisure while leaving its practical limits unstated.
evidence: Summah's settin' on de th'one,

days.title: The little master forester — excerpt
days.challenge: Distinguish observed squirrel behaviour, estimated quantities and figurative claims about character.
days.focus: How a small animal can influence a forest far beyond its own size.
days.context: Muir introduces the Douglas squirrel, a conifer-seed eater of western North America. His affectionate human comparisons sit beside observations and explicitly qualified estimates.
days.contentNote: The passage uses a historical label for an Indigenous informant, refers to hunting and briefly mentions eating squirrel flesh. Its numerical estimates and evolutionary suggestions are historical claims to examine.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Douglas Squirrel; complete source paragraphs 435–441 in the accompanying source index; opens “The Douglas Squirrel is by far the most interesting and influential of”; closes “a sparrow; while in bluff, audacious noisiness he is a very jay.”.

questions.prompt: What actual activity supports calling the squirrel a “master forester”?
facilitatorNotes: Some buried cones and seeds are not eaten and germinate. That mechanism connects food storage to tree distribution without requiring the squirrel to intend forestry.
evidence: some of the seeds germinate and become trees.

questions.prompt: How does Muir mark the limits of his knowledge amid his confident praise?
facilitatorNotes: He says the effect of feet on growth is difficult to learn, uses “Probably” for cone proportions and presents ancestry as a suggestion. These are not all equally established facts.
evidence: How much the growth of the trees is stimulated by this means it is not easy to learn

questions.prompt: Why does the dazzling creature suddenly become a “plodding farmer”?
facilitatorNotes: Seasonal storage reveals methodical work behind spectacular movement. The change complicates the impression of effortless energy and links liveliness to preparation for winter.
evidence: examining every branch in regular order, as if careful that not one should escape him

days.title: Snowfall
days.challenge: Separate quoted judgments from the speaker’s reply and test whether outward cheer reveals inner feeling.
days.focus: Conflicting images expose the limits of knowing another person’s sorrow.
days.context: The dialogue concerns a woman whose feelings are uncertain. The hunter’s fire is a metaphor; the poem contains no hunting scene.
days.contentNote: The poem discusses hidden sadness and heartbreak.

excerpt.locator: Snowfall; complete poem, opening “"She can't be unhappy," you said,” and closing “Smothered in snow.”.

questions.prompt: Which images make the first observer confident she is happy?
facilitatorNotes: Star-like smiles and a thistledown laugh make cheer seem light and visible. The claim relies on appearance.
evidence: The smiles are like stars in her eyes,

questions.prompt: How does the speaker limit what anyone can claim about another person?
facilitatorNotes: The rhetorical question insists that people directly know only their own heartbreak. It cautions against certainty without proving the woman is unhappy.
evidence:
But who has ever known
Another's heartbreak--

questions.prompt: What can a fire smothered in snow suggest that thistledown cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Hidden heat or feeling may remain beneath a quiet surface; the contrasting image permits pain concealed by composure. Stress that this is the speaker’s impression, not confirmed access to her mind.
evidence:
Her heart were a hunter's fire
 Smothered in snow.

days.title: Cones, caches and competing collectors — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare the squirrel’s methods for different cones and examine a reversal in the language of theft.
days.focus: Food preparation, seasonal storage and human interference in the squirrel’s work.
days.context: Muir watches squirrels remove cone scales to reach seeds. “Silver First” is the wording printed in this 1894 edition, apparently a printer’s error for Silver Firs.
days.contentNote: The text describes cutting trees for commercial seed collection and taking squirrels’ stored food. It also gives a speculative explanation linking aromatic oils to the animal’s energy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, The Douglas Squirrel; complete source paragraphs 447–454 in the accompanying source index; opens “No other of the Sierra animals of my acquaintance is better fed,”; closes “his shoulder and on to the book he held in his hand.”.

questions.prompt: How does cone size change the squirrel’s harvesting method?
facilitatorNotes: Small cones are held and eaten on a branch; very large ones are dropped and dragged to a working place on the ground. In both cases it follows the spiral arrangement of scales.
evidence: the immense size of the cones of the Sugar Pine

questions.prompt: Why does he eat immature seeds but wait to fill his stores?
facilitatorNotes: The passage distinguishes immediate meals from storing mature cones in October and November. Ask readers to use that distinction without inventing an experiment the author did not perform.
evidence: wait until they are matured before he gathers them into his barns.

questions.prompt: Who is the “spoiler” when the squirrel takes cones back, and how does that wording shape sympathy?
facilitatorNotes: The seedsman has taken the squirrel’s gathered supplies; recovering them reverses the normal accusation that animals steal from people. The payment of grain acknowledges the discomfort.
evidence: the little Douglas has exhaustively spoiled the spoiler.

days.title: Winter
days.challenge: Identify each month’s distinctive personification and follow the closing couplet’s turn toward hope.
days.focus: A sequence of characters makes seasonal movement varied rather than uniformly bleak.
days.context: Rime is frost and miry means muddy. Read each month with a different voice before considering the sunbeam.

excerpt.locator: Winter; complete poem, opening “Old January, clad in crispy rime,” and closing “Its cheering promise of returning Springs.”.

questions.prompt: How is January’s movement different from February’s?
facilitatorNotes: January limps slowly and refuses to hurry; February hastens toward home in timid discomfort.
evidence: He mends no pace, but beats his dithering hand.

questions.prompt: Why does March become a prophetess rather than another weary traveler?
facilitatorNotes: Her storm-inspired vision and commands give her energetic, almost visionary power; she seems to announce change.
evidence: Then March, the prophetess, by storms inspired,

questions.prompt: How does the sunbeam resist the poem’s darkest weather?
facilitatorNotes: It appears beneath the blackest cloud, turning a small opening into a promise of future spring rather than claiming winter is already gone.
evidence: Its cheering promise of returning Springs.

days.title: A cloud of birds, then a quieter season — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow changes in viewing distance, shape and sound, then notice the seasonal turn at the end.
days.focus: How a flock is described first as weather and then as individual living voices.
days.context: A belt of fir trees borders the ash copse and serves as a roost. The passage begins with flocks arriving near sunset and ends with the reduced birdsong of late summer.
days.contentNote: A passing reference to the shooting season dates the seasonal change. No shooting occurs in this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: Chapter Twelve; complete source paragraphs 437–441 in the accompanying source index; opens “Clustering cones hang from the firs, fringing the copse on one”; closes “gleaming water, where a creek of the shallow lake runs in towards it.”.

questions.prompt: How does the flock’s arrival differ from the arrival of rooks?
facilitatorNotes: Starlings approach in separate groups from many directions, whereas rooks return in long streams. This contrast helps the reader visualize the gathering rather than merely its large size.
evidence: Rooks, in returning to roost fly in long streams, starlings in numerous separate divisions.

questions.prompt: What breaks the initial illusion that a dark cloud hangs over the copse?
facilitatorNotes: The apparent cloud contracts, pours into trees and rises again; approaching it reveals countless calling birds. Both motion and closer perception revise the first impression.
evidence: this apparent cloud is found to consist of thousands of starlings

questions.prompt: Does the passage end in complete silence? How does the qualification affect its mood?
facilitatorNotes: Robin, wood-pigeon and greenfinch still call, but less abundantly than before. The quiet is relative, making the observer attentive to small remaining sounds rather than presenting the landscape as lifeless.
evidence: It is not absolute silence indeed; but the difference is very noticeable.

days.title: Move eastward, happy earth...
days.challenge: Distinguish the speaker’s personal impatience from the planet-wide movement invoked to satisfy it.
days.focus: Cosmic scale magnifies the anticipation of a marriage day.
days.context: The silver sister-world is the moon in the poem’s imagery.

excerpt.locator: Move eastward, happy earth...; complete poem, opening “Move eastward, happy earth, and leave” and closing “And round again to happy night.”.

questions.prompt: How does addressing the earth turn waiting into an appeal for action?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated imperatives ask the whole planet to carry the speaker toward a desired time.
evidence: O, happy planet, eastward go;

questions.prompt: What connection joins the moon with the watching eyes below?
facilitatorNotes: The moon is imagined reflected in dewy eyes, bringing distant celestial light into an intimate scene.
evidence: To glass herself in dewy eyes

questions.prompt: Why end by asking for both marriage morning and happy night?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker imagines a complete desired day rather than only sunrise. The ordinary cycle is emotionally transformed by anticipation.
evidence: And move me to my marriage-morn,

days.title: A wind-storm in the forest, part 1 — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare the observer’s excitement with details that disclose danger, then track his choice of viewpoint.
days.focus: How individual trees become visible through their contrasting movements and sounds.
days.context: In December 1874 Muir leaves a friend’s house during a strong wind. This first part follows his walk and ends when he reaches a treetop; the next part continues the same episode.
days.contentNote: Muir climbs a tall tree during a violent windstorm and describes his own judgment of the risk.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, A Wind-Storm in the Forest; complete source paragraphs 470–473 in the accompanying source index; opens “One of the most beautiful and exhilarating storms I ever enjoyed in”; closes “I clung with muscles firm braced, like a bobolink on a reed.”.

questions.prompt: Which details complicate Muir’s reassuring comparison with staying indoors?
facilitatorNotes: Trees are falling every few minutes; saturated ground and old fire damage cause failures. His personal confidence does not cancel those observed hazards.
evidence: I heard trees falling for hours at the rate of one every two or three minutes

questions.prompt: Why does Muir emphasize individual voices within the loud “anthem”?
facilitatorNotes: He can distinguish species and even grass among the combined sounds. This supports his claim that the forest contains varied characters, not one uniform mass.
evidence: I could distinctly hear the varying tones of individual trees

questions.prompt: What three considerations influence his choice of a climbing tree?
facilitatorNotes: He considers stability and neighbouring falls, whether its trunk can be climbed, and whether it affords a view. These explain his reasoning without proving the choice safe.
evidence: while others were not favorably situated for clear views.

days.title: A wind-storm in the forest, part 2 — excerpt
days.challenge: Track how sight, sound and smell support a widening reflection about travel and memory.
days.focus: How moving trees and travelling scents change the observer’s understanding of a familiar forest.
days.context: Continuing the preceding episode, Muir is perched near the top of a swaying Douglas spruce. He observes the forest from there before descending as the wind subsides.
days.contentNote: This continues a dangerous storm climb. The observer’s claims of safety and of trees enjoying the storm are his interpretation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, A Wind-Storm in the Forest; complete source paragraphs 475–485 in the accompanying source index; opens “In its widest sweeps my tree-top described an arc of from twenty”; closes “before did these noble woods appear so fresh, so joyous, so immortal.”.

questions.prompt: How do waves become a useful comparison for the light on the forest?
facilitatorNotes: Wind turns needles so that reflected light appears to move across successive groves, breaking and reforming like surf. The analogy explains both the motion and its shimmering appearance.
evidence: as the shining foliage was stirred by corresponding waves of air.

questions.prompt: Why does a sea breeze in Florida briefly take Muir back to Scotland?
facilitatorNotes: A recognized smell recalls childhood after nineteen inland years. He uses personal memory to support the broader claim that winds carry information from places they touch.
evidence: which at once awakened and set free a thousand dormant associations

questions.prompt: What makes the claim that trees are travellers more than a joke?
facilitatorNotes: They move with Earth through space and make shorter bending journeys in the wind. Comparing these with people’s return trips challenges a simple boundary between rooted and travelling lives.
evidence: our own little journeys, away and back again, are only little more than tree-wavings

days.title: The Poet’s Song
days.challenge: Follow a sequence of interrupted animal actions and infer why the imagined song attracts such a varied audience.
days.focus: The poem dramatizes art’s power through listeners’ reactions while withholding the song’s actual words.
days.context: The animals’ listening is imaginative personification, not a claim about animal behavior.
days.contentNote: A hawk is shown with its foot on prey; no injury is described.

excerpt.locator: The Poet’s Song; complete poem, opening “The rain had fallen, the Poet arose,” and closing “When the years have died away”.”.

questions.prompt: How do moving shadows over wheat prepare a scene already full of rhythm?
facilitatorNotes: The landscape has waves and wind before the poet sings, linking the human melody with natural motion.
evidence: And waves of shadow went over the wheat,

questions.prompt: Why show birds and a hawk stopping activities instead of merely calling the song beautiful?
facilitatorNotes: Their interruptions give the song a visible effect across different creatures; even a predator’s attention changes.
evidence: And stared, with his foot on the prey,

questions.prompt: What does the nightingale tell us about the song, and what does it leave unknown?
facilitatorNotes: It says the song imagines a future world and surpasses its own songs in gladness, but gives no actual lyrics or detailed future. Do not fill that gap with an invented utopia.
evidence: For he sings of what the world will be

days.title: Old Poesy
days.challenge: Trace a critical argument through contrasting living flowers and manufactured imitations, rather than reading it as a neutral history.
days.focus: The speaker values feeling and vitality over fashionable technical display.
days.context: Poesy means poetry; a magic-lanthorn projects images and an automaton imitates living motion. These objects serve as comparisons, not instructions.

excerpt.locator: Old Poesy; complete poem, opening “Sweet is the poesy of the olden time,” and closing “Shadows of life, and artificial flowers.”.

questions.prompt: What does old poetry supposedly give to stocks and stones?
facilitatorNotes: It gives them speech and life through imagination, showing the power the speaker admires.
evidence: A soul of utterance and a tongue of life.

questions.prompt: Why describe the rejected poems as wild flowers treated as weeds?
facilitatorNotes: The same thing can be dismissed by fashion yet prized by the speaker. The image makes value depend on the observer’s standard.
evidence: Which Art and Fashion fling as weeds away,

questions.prompt: Does the poem prove all newer poetry is worse?
facilitatorNotes: It offers a forceful preference through living-versus-artificial imagery, not a survey of every work. Readers can question the generalization while explaining its persuasive comparisons.
evidence: Shadows of life, and artificial flowers.

days.title: The work of a mountain thunderstorm — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a storm’s brief sequence, then connect its effects to a much longer history of the landscape.
days.focus: How a destructive-looking event also becomes an account of water nourishing many forms of life.
days.context: Muir begins with a small typical summer storm and then recalls a much larger storm near Yosemite in July 1869. The descriptions and measurements belong to this historical account.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, Sierra Thunder-Storms; complete source paragraphs 503–506 in the accompanying source index; opens “The weather of spring and summer in the middle region of the”; closes “river, mountain and valley—all that the landscape holds—reflected in their crystal depths.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the smallest storm seem complete even though it is so brief?
facilitatorNotes: One cloud develops, lightning strikes, rain falls and the sky clears, leaving washed air and refreshed ground. The tight sequence makes a miniature whole.
evidence: one cloud, one lightning-stroke, and one dash of rain.

questions.prompt: How does the remembered 1869 storm complicate the opening picture of gentle renewal?
facilitatorNotes: Lightning splits enormous firs and rain covers the ground; the storm can damage as well as refresh. Muir’s admiration includes its force.
evidence: were split into long rails and slivers from top to bottom

questions.prompt: Why end by comparing half-drop flower cups with lake basins?
facilitatorNotes: The scale changes radically, but both receive water. The closing image connects individual drops to an interdependent landscape rather than treating rain as background weather.
evidence: cassiope-cups, holding half a drop, and lake basins between the hills

days.title: Autumn
days.challenge: Sustain attention across many short stanzas while tracing competing moods of pleasure, grief, and anticipated renewal.
days.focus: The season is a changing companion whose decline does not erase its beauty.
days.context: Read once for the walk’s sights and again for addresses to Autumn. Seasonal death and burial images are personifications, not a narrative of a person’s death.
days.contentNote: Uses non-graphic death and burial imagery for the ending of a season.

excerpt.locator: Autumn; complete poem, opening “Syren of sullen moods and fading hues,” and closing “Awake to glories new.”.

questions.prompt: How does happy though I sigh prepare the rest of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It openly joins emotions often treated as opposites; later beauty and decline continue that mixed response.
evidence: And happy, though I sigh.

questions.prompt: Why include the startled hare and its eventual refuge?
facilitatorNotes: The movement from mowing danger to calm shelter complicates a merely decorative rural scene. Creaturely experience is part of the season’s world.
evidence: And lull to calm repose.

questions.prompt: Does the ending make Autumn’s grave final?
facilitatorNotes: The last return to awakening places decline inside a cycle. The grief is not erased, but future glory changes its meaning.
evidence: Awake to glories new.
